Sports.title: Spain players slapped with huge bill immediately after World Cup final win over Argentina
Sports.content:
Spain players slapped with huge bill immediately after World Cup final win over Argentina

The Spain national team's historic World Cup feat was followed by having to pay a mammoth bill

View 2 Images Spain's World Cup heroes have been taxed heavily following Sunday's historic victory (Image: Getty )

Spain’s World Cup heroes have been hit with a hefty tax bill after their 1-0 victory over Argentina in the final. Luis de la Fuente’s side dominated proceedings at the MetLife Stadium on Sunday night and were justly rewarded with an extra-time winner courtesy of Ferran Torres.

‌



For the 26-man Spain squad, nothing will quite match the euphoria of adding a second star above their nation’s badge. Yet, they certainly would have welcomed the huge financial boost they received for lifting the iconic golden trophy from the Royal Spanish Football Federation (RFEF).

‌



According to Gestha, the Spanish union representing Tax Agency experts, each player is set to receive a gross payout of €754,701.92 (£640,500) for winning the World Cup. The sum aligns with the agreement reached with RFEF, under which the players were to receive 45% of the prize money FIFA awards to the governing body for winning the tournament - a total sum of around €44million (£37.3m).

‌



JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

Full list of Argentina's 27 dirty tricks in World Cup final as they ruin greatest match READ MORE :

As a result, around €19.8m (£16.8m) will go to the players, after reportedly agreeing to only collect major bonuses if they reached the latter rounds.

However, the players immediately had to part ways with a significant chunk of that cash due to income tax. Depending on where they play their club football, the Spanish players’ personal income tax reaches 49.5 per cent, and in others it is around 45 per cent, amounting to each player losing a maximum of €370,000 (£314,000) to tax.

‌



The 17 squad members currently playing their football in Spain are subject to the country's prevailing personal income tax (IRPF) regulations, specifically those of the particular Autonomous Community where they reside.

Given the high income levels typical of these players, the entire bonus falls into the highest marginal tax bracket. Since personal income tax combines state and regional scales, the tax burden depends on the individual's region of residence, of which there are 17.

In some instances, such as the Community of Madrid, the marginal rate reportedly hovers around 45%, though it can exceed 50% in certain regions. It stands at 49% in the Basque Country, while in Catalonia, home to a significant number of players, it ranges from 47% to 49.5%.

‌



View 2 Images Spain's players each received a gross payment of £640,500 for winning the World Cup (Image: Getty )

That is to say, in the best-case scenario, an international player competing in Spain would receive a total of €385,000 (£327,000) in bonus payments. If the rate rises to 49.5%, that figure drops to €353,500 (£300,000).

The list of players required to declare these amounts under these strict conditions includes names from the elite of Spanish football, such as Lamine Yamal, Dani Olmo, Pau Cubarsi, Eric Garcia, Joan Garcia, Marc Pubill, Ferran Torres, Pedri, and Gavi. Spain's public treasury will be delighted, with members of the squad playing in the Spanish league paying a total of around £5m in taxes.

Article continues below

The situation is different for international players competing in foreign leagues, such as Mikel Merino, Pedro Porro, Martin Zubimendi, David Raya, Victor Munoz, Fabian Ruiz and Rodri. They are subject to the tax laws of the country where they are tax residents (England or France) and to double taxation treaties. In addition to this are the taxes levied in the three host countries of this World Cup: the United States, Mexico, and Portugal.

While the reward for their success is substantial, it is not necessarily as large as one might expect given the historic achievement for the country, especially considering that the bonuses distributed to the players for the 2010 World Cup were around €600,000 (£503,000).

Sports.title: All 37 World Cup pundits ranked as BBC vs ITV winner decided and unexpected star emerges
Sports.content:
All 37 World Cup pundits ranked as BBC vs ITV winner decided and unexpected star emerges

World Cup 2026 is now in the books and it's safe to say some pundits proved their value, while others left fans utterly underwhelmed over the past five weeks

View 9 Images Wayne Rooney emerged as a star among World Cup 2026 pundits and was among the BBC's finest contributors (Image: BBC Sport)

This summer's World Cup proved to be the feast of football fans wanted but the on-field stars are nothing without the pundits calling the action. ITV and the BBC once again went to war in their quadrennial tug-of-war, each featuring a star-studded array of commentators and broadcasting talent.

‌



Except not every ex-pro or manager on the panel was necessarily worthy of the investment as Spain pipped Argentina to the top prize. At the same time, other new names in the punditry arena emerged as the stars of tomorrow and will undoubtedly be back on our screens come 2030.

‌



From historic moments illustrated in real time to bizarre accounts of cat-nappings, World Cup 2026 had a little bit of everything.

‌



Mirror Football has ranked every major name to have starred over the past month-and-a-half, as well as deciding who really came out on top between the Beeb and ITV productions.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

John Cross’ alternative World Cup awards as FIFA bosses called out for huge mistake READ MORE :

Argentina facing double punishment after 'disgusting' scenes in World Cup final defeat READ MORE :

BBC

Wayne Rooney: 8.5/10

‌



If there was already growing sentiment Wayne Rooney is a sleeping giant of the punditry scene, Sunday's final was his awakening. And it gave us a true glimpse of the grump at his best, mocking the half-time performance as "c**p" while his BBC colleagues fawned over the display in New Jersey.

That was just the icing on the cake of what was otherwise an insightful, informative and consistently interesting contribution from the Manchester United icon, however. Not to mention Rooney showed what a good sport he was by (kind of) adhering to his wager with Erling Haaland by rowing down the Hudson River.

England's former all-time top scorer was succinct in his analysis but knows exactly when a situation calls for some levity. He also ensured he'll be on the right side of history by criticising the FIFA shambles surrounding Folarin Balogun's red card being suspended for the Belgium encounter.

‌



Danny Murphy: 4/10

It was the most caricatured 'bored English pundit' sentence on record and one that will never leave Danny Murphy. We're of course talking about the ex-midfielder's missing cat, Bob, and the bizarre mid-match story no-one ever asked for.

"I used to have a cat called Bob," said Murphy while commentating on Norway's round-of-32 win over the Ivory Coast, seemingly inspired by Norwegian winger Oscar Bobb. "He jumped into the back of a Royal Mail van, and we lost him."

‌



A moment as fleeting as our connection to the cat in question, who was later found before being adopted by friends of his family, Murphy revealed. It says a lot about his punditry that this will be what his World Cup is remembered for most.

The BBC clearly enjoyed the unintentionally iconic piece of punditry, too, after 'Bob the Cat' was credited as its 'Commentary Mascot' in the broadcaster's closing montage.

Content cannot be displayed without consent

‌



Cesar Azpilicueta: 7.5/10

The only complaint one might make of Cesar Azpilicueta's performance over the past five weeks is that fans may have liked to hear a little more from him. However, there's perhaps only so much one can expect from an ex-pro speaking in their second language (or third, given Azpilicueta is also fluent in French).

That said, the ex-Chelsea captain was intuitive in his assessments, particularly when commenting on defensive structure. Had he gone on the offensive himself a little more, Azpilicueta might have broken into the top bracket of World Cup pundits himself.

‌



Get the latest World Cup news straight to your inbox by signing up to our Make Football Great Again newsletter now!

Steph Houghton: 7/10

There are few more experienced England players the BBC could have called upon than former Lionesses captain Steph Houghton. And the Manchester City great duly delivered, coming off well on screen and, like Azpilicueta, strutting her knowledge in particular around the defensive side of the game.

‌



Joe Hart: 8.5/10

View 9 Images Joe Hart did not look out of place among more experienced pundits (Image: BBC)

Arguably the British breakout star of the entire tournament and one we look forward to seeing a lot more of on screens in future. In Joe Hart, Micah Richards finally has a foil willing to bring the same spirited energy and affable quality to his football coverage.

‌



The ex-England goalkeeper's passion for the tournament was contagious but he consistently brought the tools able to back it up in his breakdowns. And not only in regards to those between the posts, providing potent pearls of wisdom on tactics and the thought processes players might be experiencing under pressure.

Hart showed he was up for any and every challenge by helping former team-mate Rooney with his row down the Hudson. Ironically, he got much wetter performing a pre-World Cup final preview in New York, where he was drenched in torrential conditions and even lost his shoes.

Ashley Williams: 6/10

‌



Fairly middle of the road among BBC contributors, Ashley Williams was...fine. There's nothing to knock about the Wales great's analysis, particularly when discussing his preferred arena in defence, but there simply wasn't enough charisma or confidence in his efforts to stand out among a crowd of more impassioned peers.

Content cannot be displayed without consent

Thomas Frank: 8.5/10

‌



When Thomas Frank speaks about football, there's a sense you need to listen out of fear you could quickly miss out on a gem of tactical treasure. Arguably the Dane's greatest quality is his ability to put complicated concepts into terms even those without a UEFA licence can easily interpret.

Unlike more former managers, Frank is also likeable due to the fact he's also a lot more candid and forthcoming with his passion for the sport. It may not have been sufficient to make for success at Spurs but he may have found a new calling.

Lucas Leiva: 5/10

‌



One would have been forgiven missing Lucas Leiva's cameos during this World Cup. And that goes as much for those who were actually watching those games he actually worked for the BBC.

Again, it can be more difficult to judge those who may not feel as comfortable not speaking in their first language. However, the Liverpool fan favourite was nonetheless overly cautious and therefore didn't contribute much.

Unlucky.

‌



Olivier Giroud: 5.5/10

View 9 Images Olivier Giroud looked the part but at times sounded slightly out of his depth (Image: BBC)

If the World Cup pundits were ranked on looks alone, there's a high chance Olivier Giroud may be the only one to walk away with full marks. As it is, however, his breakdown of what was happening on-field was sorely lacking and received criticism from plenty of supporters online.

‌



The former Chelsea and Arsenal frontman gets brownie points for certain insights on the France squad, which he was still part of in the not-too-distant past. Everything else was médiocre (mediocre).

Gael Clichy: 7.5/10

On the other hand, fellow Arsenal alumnus Gael Clichy perhaps turned a lot of surprised heads with how effective he was at times. Much like he was as a player, the retired left-back was no-nonsense and showed plenty of conviction in his comments, with a welcome sprinkle of anecdotes from his own career.

‌



Ellen White: 8.5/10

It was hard not to like Ellen White as a player; now arguably even more so as a pundit. As fans stayed up for some of the less attractive early-hours kick-offs, the highest goalscorer in the history of the Lionesses gave a much-needed push of positivity.

As is only natural for the former Chelsea and Arsenal poacher, White's main area of expertise lent itself well to breaking down striker movement and the like. Went about her work with confidence and was consistently engaging for viewers when she did appear.

‌



Thomas Hitzelsperger: 8/10

It was almost cruel to watch Thomas Hitzelsperger oversee Germany's demise live as they exited at Paraguayan hands in the last 32. However, his candid commentary only added to his appeal as he refused to sugarcoat his own team's shortcomings.

Add to that his jewels of wisdom on all things midfield-related and you have the makings of a very strong performance for the BBC.

‌



Netflix

Gary Lineker: 8/10

View 9 Images Gary Lineker's Netflix World Cup coverage offered audiences a very different feel (Image: Netflix)

Netflix's World Cup production became something of a third wheel to the BBC versus ITV drama that took centre stage. However, it inevitably had a reliable captain steering the ship in Gary Lineker.

‌



The Leicester City legend contributed to a slightly unorthodox alternative on the streaming service. It worked in its own way but was inevitably overshadowed by its terrestrial counterparts.

That's more a matter of exposure, however, as Lineker himself was characteristically solid and gave his usual above-average display. He even added his own bit to the soap opera by making cameos on both ITV and BBC productions, gatecrashing Richards on the latter following England's memorable win over Norway.

Joe Cole: 6/10

‌



You sometimes got the impression that Joe Cole began breaking things down without fully knowing the destination he was trying to reach. The ex-Chelsea trickster gets kudos for being the relatable man on the ground but his analysis often left you with more questions than before he started speaking.

Netflix also hosted a somewhat awkward moment when he hinted the World Cup was at risk of appearing rigged for a certain Lionel Messi to win.

John Mikel Obi: 7.5/10

‌



The man who called out former team-mate Cole for his allusion to a Messi fix, John Mikel Obi called it as he saw it. That clash with Cole in particular made for good viewing as he passionately defended his own stance and called out the Cristiano Ronaldo boo boys.

Mikel also has a likeable habit of coming out with truly intriguing points not raised by his colleagues. And that podcast feel to his approach made for a heartening fireside-chat style of punditry.

Micah Richards: 8/10

‌



View 9 Images Micah Richards offered his usual injection of energy for multiple broadcasters at World Cup 2026 (Image: Netflix)

Performing a dual role on Netflix and the BBC, Richards somehow managed to maintain his unparalleled punditry passion across all mediums. Simply put, it's hard to come away from a production when Richards is part of the ride without coming round to the excited kid sat among usually more demure cast members.

Sure, he may not come close to matching the intricate analysis displayed by the Thomas Franks of the world. But the current British football scene would be a lot poorer were it not for his input, even if it is oriented more for the TikTok generation.

‌



Points lost for suggesting the disgraceful Leandro Paredes was "better than" the red card antics witnessed during and after the World Cup final. The Argentinian's long history of bullying tactics would suggest otherwise.

Alan Shearer: 7/10

Like Richards, Shearer was on the books for the BBC alongside his appearances with The Rest Is Football crew. And his commentary gave the usual brutally honest soundbites that tend to go down well with British fans.

‌



The Newcastle icon loses some points for being almost too dour at points, however, not quite catching the balance between thought-provoking and just downright grouchy.

ITV

Roy Keane: 8.5/10

View 9 Images Roy Keane brought humour and insight in equal measure at this World Cup (Image: ITV)

‌



The most un-Roy Keane performance at a major tournament to date as he continues to move away from the disappointed dad display. And it only makes for an even more engaging version of the Irishman's usually pithy persona.

That's not to say Keane's crushing critiques didn't still appear in packed punches when relevant. However, he continues to demonstrate there are more strings to his bow, breaking down player mentality more so than anything in valuable measure.

When Keane appeared on ITV, you tended to perk up and usually for good reason. If that's not the sign of a pundit worth listening to, we don't know what is.

‌



Gary Neville: 7.5/10

A more downbeat Gary Neville than fans are perhaps used to seeing. He even outscored long-time colleague Keane in the grump stakes, which takes some doing.

Amid the sea of critiques it's often possible to make about England at major tournament, there are routinely more positives worth focusing on. Neville fiercely represented that inclination to lean into the gloom and it more often than not made for unattractive viewing.

‌



In keeping with that theme, his touch of realism did come in handy with one pre-tournament prediction that exhibited his nous. That being his premonition that the Three Lions would struggle to keep possession against the top teams, just as they did in the closing stages of their exit to Argentina.

Ally McCoist: 7/10

In direct contrast to that style, Ally McCoist brought his usual golden retriever-esque charm to proceedings. There's arguably no-one in the punditry community who audibly enjoys a well-struck ball as much as the Scottish icon.

‌



Too often do some pundits get lost in the weeds of tactics and come out sounding like they don't entirely know what they're saying. McCoist rarely gets too deep into the minute details but his undying love for the game is infectious in itself.

Emma Hayes: 9.5/10

View 9 Images Ex-Chelsea women's coach Emma Hayes was the best pundit at World Cup 2026 (Image: ITV)

‌



Acting as a foil to Keane's contributions around character and moxy (or lack thereof), Emma Hayes starred as ITV's tactical whiz time and time again. The only complaint around her nous is that we perhaps didn't get to see enough of it.

Should we be surprised? The United States boss and seven-time WSL winner at Chelsea has dominated women's coaching for more than a decade and nonchalantly conjures up the kind of tactical tidbits that make you realise why.

If ITV knows what it's doing, it will lock Hayes - who also worked on the Netflix production - down for future tournaments and get her in front of that whiteboard with increasing regularity.

‌



Ian Wright: 8.5/10

Another who offers passion in inexhaustible quantities, Ian Wright was yet again a star of the ITV production. If he wasn't getting you excited during build-up or half-time breaks, the Arsenal great's activities around the ITV base in Brooklyn made for a superb sideshow.

He's a man England fans can rally around given he always seems to represent the everyman sentiment in the professional scene. Best of all, however, he actually knows his football and brings viewers into the fold with shrewd understanding.

‌



Bradley Wright-Phillips: 7/10

It was a clever move by ITV to rope in Bradley Wright-Phillips as a father-and-son act that would have made Stavros Flately envious. As a Major League Soccer icon, the New York Red Bulls icon did a fine job acting as a conduit between the US and UK sides of the spectrum.

Patrick Vieira: 8.5/10

‌



He may not have the sense of humour of a Keane, but Patrick Vieira has also moved handily from his midfield enforcer role as a pundit. What's more, his tactical analysis is up there with the best of the tournament, which should come as no surprise for one who's prioritised the move into management.

That's not to say the Frenchman isn't without his funny moments and he bounces particularly off former arch-nemesis Keane. As was the case throughout his playing career, there's not really anything one can say 'Pat' does badly.

Ange Postecoglou: 9/10

‌



View 9 Images Ange Postecoglou entertained and educated this summer (Image: The Overlap)

Another masterstroke by ITV was adding the cerebral mind of Ange Postecoglou to its ranks this summer. As one might expect from a man who cut his teeth managing in lower-profile leagues like Japan and Australia, there didn't seem to be a nation Postecoglou wasn't informed on.

Whatever the fixture, the former Spurs and Celtic boss had something insightful to contribute. Add to that the fact he comes across as a genuinely likeable human and the new Al-Nassr coach makes for an extremely potent punditry package.

‌



Lee Dixon: 3.5/10

Truly, there may never have been an ex-pro who sounded so disappointed to be working at a World Cup. Lee Dixon's monotone musings on matchday duties often gave the impression he would have preferred to be called up for jury service than featuring at the biggest sporting event on the planet.

Karen Carney: 7/10

‌



Karen Carney continuously demonstrates she has the tactical nous to interpret the game as well as most peers despite what online trolls might say. The England centurion clearly tried to inject positivity when fixtures were sometimes feeling flat, albeit lacking a little of that human touch that makes the likes of Wright and Hayes so likeable.

Jobi McAnuff: 8/10

A somewhat unexpected star of the World Cup when called upon. Again, Jobi McAnuff was mostly relegated to certain late kick-offs and therefore may have gone unnoticed by many but his deep research into his work came across well.

‌



There should be no surprises the retired Reading winger's delivery was top notch, too.

Duncan Ferguson: 7/10

Sticking with that theme of surprise packages, Duncan Ferguson's World Cup samples were also hard not to enjoy when he did appear. As one might expect, the honourary Evertonian was certainly not lacking in confidence, which made for smooth watching as he put those around him at ease.

‌



Andros Townsend: 7/10

Andros Townsend gave certain spectators a laugh when he referred to MK Dons (one of his former clubs) as a 'franchise' before immediately apologising to ITV viewers. Albeit not for ITV, Townsend also took it upon himself to produce self-made content on TikTok showcasing his analysis skills and was absolutely on the money, veering away from the anti-Thomas Tuchel narrative.

FOX

Thierry Henry: 8.5/10

‌



View 9 Images FOX was lucky to have Thierry Henry as a pundit (Image: Fox Sports)

World Cup fans in the UK may understandably feel some pangs of regret that Thierry Henry isn't signed up to one of the British broadcasters. Their loss has been FOX's gain and the American production benefits massively from the Frenchman's pure approach.

Another of those examples that when he speaks, you tend to perk up your ears. And 1998 World Cup-winner Henry is a particularly valuable resource to the 'soccer' crowd overseas given he's an all-time great who can pick the game apart in relatable and often almost poetic terms.

‌



Alexi Lalas: 3/10

Without doing too much of a disservice to one of US football's biggest broadcasting champions of the 21st century, Alexi Lalas too often looked out of his depth at this World Cup. Surrounded by genuine icons of the game, it too often came across as though he was trying to educate far more celebrated peers rather than handing them the platforms they deserve.

Rio Ferdinand: 6.5/10

‌



Rio Ferdinand was only a minor cast member of the FOX production as he appeared on James Corden's spin-off show over the tournament. That being said, he had his value as a boots-on-the-ground member of the team and his passion for the England cause came across well.

Zlatan Ibrahimovic: 8/10

Content cannot be displayed without consent

‌



Again, FOX orchestrated a masterstroke by pairing the infatiguable calm of Zlatan Ibrahimovic with the boyish charm of Henry. Always good for a soundbite, Zlatan made his major broadcasting debut in a way that had even fans outside the US wanting to keep up with the FOX team.

That nonchalance comes at a cost, though, and Ibrahimovic at times seemed overly reliant on being funny rather than offering genuine insights. However, his hilarious 'Who?' response to Lalas' absence from one broadcast will live long in this World Cup's memory.

Thiago Alcantara: 7.5/10

‌



A potential star in the making if his commitment to coaching doesn't take him too far outside the punditry bubble. As one might only expect, Thiago Alcantara's analysis and ability to spot trends others did not marked him out as a true disciple of Pep Guardiola.

Clint Dempsey: 8/10

If Alexi Lalas showcased a certain level of arrogance from the US perspective, Clint Dempsey exemplified the much more relatable stance from across the pond. A modern great for the Stars and Stripes, 'Deuce' sounded confident in his work without verging into cockiness, particularly when celebrating the United States' early achievements.

‌



Clarence Seedorf: 8.5/10

The older head in the room that made even the likes of Henry and Ibrahimovic tilt their caps out of respect. If there's one thing that has come across over the past month-and-a-half of FOX television, it's that Clarence Seedorf knows ball.

The Dutchman seamlessly unpacked plays in scientific detail without it sounding like a chore to those at home. A rare combination of craftsmanship and character, every voyage that had Seedorf aboard was inherently more enjoyable to watch.

‌



BBC vs ITV Verdict

The BBC got its World Cup coverage off to a poor start after it emerged the production team wouldn't even be in the States for the entirety of the group stage. ITV, by contrast, unveiled a sprawling Brooklyn set that made viewers feel like they were close to the action from start to finish.

Visuals aside, the overall selection of contributors and median performance was also better on ITV's behalf. Additions like Hayes and Postecoglou in particular added fresh, incisive elements to the equation, while promoting talents like McAnuff showed its ability to spot rising talent.

World Cup 2026 champion: ITV

Sports.title: Man Utd land £8m teenage star from Premier League rivals as they repeat transfer trick
Sports.content:
Man Utd land £8m teenage star from Premier League rivals as they repeat transfer trick

Manchester United have secured the signing of teenager Tynan Thompson, who has joined from fellow Premier League side Tottenham for an initial £4million

View 2 Images Tynan Thompson has signed for Man United

Manchester United have landed teenage winger Tynan Thompson from Tottenham after agreeing a deal worth up to £8million.

‌



The 18-year-old has joined for an initial £4m, with a further £4m coming in potential add-ons. Thompson joined Tottenham's academy when he was 12 and continued to impress last term, which saw him twice included in Champions League matchday squads.

‌



The England youth international was a hit in the UEFA Youth League, where he scored seven goals in seven games for Tottenham, including a hat-trick in the 9-1 win over Slavia Praha.

‌



It is understood that those in Manchester have told him he will get the chance to force his way into the first-team picture, but he's poised to begin his time in the U21s.

The deal for Thompson includes a 15% sell-on clause with the MEN reporting that the add-ons are relate to the teenager's possible first-team achievements with the Red Devils.

Lisandro Martinez in floods of tears as Man Utd star suffers World Cup final agony READ MORE :

In announcing the signing, a United statement said: "Manchester United have agreed the signing of exciting young winger Tynan Thompson, subject to registration. The England youth international has joined from Tottenham Hotspur.

‌



"The 18-year-old scored 13 goals and contributed six assists last season across Under-18s to Under-21s level, including seven goals in seven UEFA Youth League games. His performances earned him opportunities within Spurs’ first-team matchday squads. Everyone at United would like to welcome Tynan to the club and wish him the very best of luck for the future."

Thompson and his family were keen to relocate and the move to Manchester presented them with that opportunity. He becomes the second teenage talent to swap north London for the north west in recent years.

View 2 Images Ayden Heaven moved to Manchester from Arsenal last year (Image: (Photo by Ash Donelon/Manchester United via Getty Images))

‌



In February last year United signed defender Ayden Heaven from Arsenal on a four-and-a-half-year contract. The teenager cost an undisclosed compensation fee and immediately linked up with the first-team squad, and has since been a big hit when given a chance.

Last year, when injuries stuck, the centre-half made 18 appearances, with all but one of those coming in the Premier League. He played every minute in wins over Chelsea, Brentford and Liverpool towards the latter end of the season.

Sports.title: Rohit shrugs off retirement chat as he plans to play on through the 'noise'
Sports.content:
India great Rohit Sharma has shrugged off talk about his international future after scoring a century against England in the ODI series decider at Lord's.

Rumours emerged during India's defeat in the second ODI at Cardiff on Thursday that the 39-year-old could be close to retirement with the Lord's fixture a possible farewell, although that was then denied by BCCI secretary Devajit Saikia.

Rohit went on to score 138 versus England, his 34th ODI hundred, but could not prevent India from slipping to a 2-1 series defeat, hot on the heels of a 4-0 T20 drubbing.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports pundit Ravi Shastri says Rohit 'shut everyone up' with his century against England after rumours of him being phased out of the ODI side

Speaking to bcci.tv after the game, Rohit said: "Look, my job is with the bat. Come and play, represent my country, represent the team. That's what I've been told to do since I made my debut so that's what I'm going to do.

"The noise since I made my debut was there and till the time I'm going to stay here, it's always going to be there, so it doesn't really matter too much.

"What matters is what I do on the field: try and contribute to the success of the team. That's all my focus is right now. And let the noise be there. If there's no noise, there's no fun. My job is inside, their job is outside. That's how I look at it."

India captain Shubman Gill said after the final ODI that there had been no indication from Rohit that he was set to end an ODI career that has seen him amass nearly 12,000 runs across 288 matches, including three double centuries.

Image: Rohit's Lords hundred featured 17 fours and five sixes

Gill told reporters: "He has not told us anything. I think it is all out in the media. But there's not been any discussion like that in the team."

The 2027 50-over World Cup would seem the perfect stage for Rohit, who turns 40 in April, to end his career, although that decision could be taken out of his hands by selectors.

The right-hander, who quit T20 international cricket in 2024 and retired from the Test arena a year later, registered scores of 11 and 26 against England prior to his Lord's ton.

Sports.title: Guardiola holds talks over Italy head coach role
Sports.content:
The Italian Football Federation (FIGC) has met with Pep Guardiola to convince him to take over as national team head coach, according to Sky in Italy.

Paolo Maldini, the new technical director of the FIGC, and Leonardo, his advisor, travelled to Barcelona to speak with the former Man City boss.

It remains to be seen if Guardiola wants the job, but the FIGC is making concrete attempts to bring him in as the national boss.

Other candidates for the role are Roberto Mancini and Andrea Pirlo.

Maldini and Leonardo spoke with Guardiola over three days, explaining their project for the Italian national team.

The FIGC brought in Maldini and Leonardo as part of a huge shake-up in Italian football following their failure to qualify for a third consecutive World Cup.

Their task was to find a successor to Gennaro Gattuso, who left his role after missing out on qualification for this summer's tournament in North America.

Guardiola is a free agent for the first time in a decade after ending his 10-year association with Manchester City. He won 20 trophies during his time at the club and finished with a win ratio of 70.8 per cent.

Italy have failed to qualify for the last three major tournaments since winning the European Championships in 2021 under Mancini.

What Guardiola said on his future after City departure

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Take a look at the best moments from Pep Guardiola's press conference after the Spaniard confirmed he would leave Man City

Speaking to Sky Sports a year before leaving the Etihad, Guardiola revealed he would be taking a break from football when the time came for his tenure at City to end.

Following the official announcement of his departure, Guardiola doubled down on this suggestion by saying that a desire to spend more time with his family was the catalyst for his decision.

"No plans for [coaching] for a while. Otherwise I would be here. I need to step back. I will not [coach] for a while," he said during his final Manchester City press conference.

"I feel I will not have the energy every day, with expectations to fight for the title. I know myself, I have that energy, but I feel like I will not have it [in the future]."

Speaking exclusively with Sky Sports, he added: "There are things that I have not done that I want to do. I still have my father alive. I want to spend more time with him. My kids... And a lot of things as a human being I can do. I'm fortunate I can decide, that's why I took this decision."

What about England?

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Jack Gaughan looks at what the future may hold for Pep Guardiola following his Manchester City departure and suggests that a future role within the England national team shouldn't be ruled out

It was widely reported in 2024 that Guardiola had reached a verbal agreement with the FA to replace Gareth Southgate as the new England boss. However, he had a change of heart and opted to stay in Manchester, as Thomas Tuchel was eventually appointed, guiding England to their best World Cup finish on foreign soil.

Tuchel is contracted until the end of Euro 2028 and has vowed to see out his new deal, which was extended in February.

What is known is that Guardiola would be interested in the challenge of moving into international management. In an interview with chef Dani Garcia in 2024, he said: "What I'm not going to do is leave Manchester City and go to another country to do the same thing as I am now.

"I wouldn't have the energy to do so. I'm still here doing what I am today. But the thought of starting somewhere else, with all the process of the training and so on... no, no, no! Maybe a national team, but that's different."

Is international management the meeting in the middle for Guardiola?

Sky Sports' Callum Bishop:

Pep Guardiola is the biggest commodity in football management. That's the case now, and that was the case when he took a break after managing Barcelona. That was followed by a move to Bayern Munich, but, as Guardiola is quick to say, he is older, lacks the energy and has too much love for Manchester City to jump into a similar job.

He has expressed an interest in spending more time with his family and resting. But we know what football obsessives are like. It doesn't take long for them to get the itch back, and Guardiola is certainly a football obsessive.

A role in international management could be enough to scratch both itches. On one hand, Guardiola wouldn't be on the training pitch day in, day out, allowing him to have the time with loved ones he desires.

However, every couple of months he could work with a group of players and teach them the Guardiola way across a Euros or World Cup cycle. Not to mention that he would be entering uncharted territory.

Having already achieved everything in club football, the switch to the international game may be incredibly appealing as it is, let alone with the improved work-life balance it offers.

Imagine if he could become the first foreign manager to guide a team to World Cup glory? It sounds far-fetched considering where Italy are right now, but if anyone can do it, it's Pep.

Sports.title: 'Rogers move is crazy money for a player Chelsea don't need!'
Sports.content:
In his latest column, Sky Sports' Paul Merson gives his reaction to Morgan Rogers' stunning £117m move to Chelsea.

Rogers is set to become Britain's most-expensive footballer ever by leaving Aston Villa this summer. He is set to sign a six-year deal, with the option of another year, at Stamford Bridge.

Read below for the Magic Man's thoughts in full about what this move means for Chelsea, Arsenal and Villa...

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Morgan Rogers has been spotted arriving for his Chelsea medical after the Blues agreed a £117m deal with Aston Villa

'I just can't see where Rogers plays'

It's a lot of money. Crazy money. Bringing Morgan Rogers in for £117m isn't what Chelsea needed.

They've got Cole Palmer! They play in the same position! Rogers went to the World Cup instead of Palmer, because they play in the same position.

Unless Chelsea go for the almighty and sell Enzo Fernandez - and swallow the pill for him, because he's not worth £100m - and then play Moises Caicedo at the base, then Rogers and Palmer both ahead of him.

But Joao Pedro is also a No 10. So with Joao Pedro, Rogers and Palmer, Chelsea have bought an attacking midfielder when they already have two very good ones.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Take a look at the best goals Morgan Rogers has scored during the 2025/26 Premier League season

Where's Palmer going to be? Stuck out on the right again? He's wasted in that position. And if Rogers is played out on the right - no disrespect, but there are a lot better right wingers than him out there.

For me, Rogers is a No 10. He's at his absolute best in open play. When the game gets broken up and he's running with the ball, he's very good at that.

But he won't get that at Chelsea. At Stamford Bridge, opposition teams kick off and sit 10 behind the ball. There's no space.

And Rogers has got to carry that price tag around with him. He will sit there and say: 'there is no pressure on me, I didn't pay that fee'. But it's a load of rubbish. Everybody will look at that when you don't do well.

A lot of people were saying it was too much for Declan Rice and Moises Caicedo when they moved for £100m. But the biggest compliment I can give them is nobody ever mentions it. They were good signings. That's what Rogers has got to hope for.

Image: Morgan Rogers will become Chelsea's most expensive player

But he's got to make things happen, which is a harder position to be in than Rice and Caicedo were. In midfield, you can do this and that - but Rogers will be judged on scoring and creating goals. That's the hardest job in the world.

I'm also sure that at the start of last season, he was atrocious for Aston Villa. I'm sure he was. Then he came good and then had a good second part of the season.

He can't play like that at Chelsea. That is an absolute no-go, it's a different ball game when you go for that kind of money.

'Arsenal need to move onto Doue or Barcola'

This move tells me that Arsenal were telling Rogers that he would play left wing, and Chelsea have told him that he will play where he wants to play, which is the No 10 role.

Image: Morgan Rogers played 45 per cent of his minutes last season as a left winger

Because I have no idea how he goes to Chelsea instead of Arsenal if they're going to play in the same position.

One team looks like they're going to win the Premier League again this year and have a good chance for the Champions League, and one team isn't even in Europe. Unless the money in the seven-year contract is mind-blowing.

Arsenal will have to now go and get another left winger. They'll have to try and get Desire Doue or Bradley Barcola from PSG. There are not a lot of wingers around, but if you want to go top, top drawer and improve what you've got, then that's what they have to get.

I cannot believe they sold Leandro Trossard by the way, I'm flabbergasted by it. They sold him for the price of a cup of tea!

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Leandro Trossard has left Premier League champions, Arsenal, for Turkish side, Besiktas

Trossard played in all the big games at the end of the season. Against the big teams, he played and he played for a reason. He's a very good footballer.

He also doesn't come across as someone who stinks the place out or kicks up a fuss when he doesn't' play. He gets on with it, comes on and does his job. I just can't believe what I've seen in that transfer, I don't get it at all.

You have to go out and buy again and buy again if you want to stay at the top. Arsenal need a few players - but they definitely need a left winger if they want to go up another level.

'What is going on at Villa? Konsa could go too...'

I just cannot believe what has happened to Aston Villa in all this.

They've just got into the Champions League, they've pulled up trees and won a European trophy. That's phenomenal for a club like Villa to do that in the same season.

But all of a sudden, they've lost their two best players in Youri Tielemans and Rogers. They're Villa's two best players by a country mile. Their two most creative players have left.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Take a look at our picks of Youri Tielemans' best Premier League goals

Tielemans was the midfielder who passed the ball, got them up the pitch, got a great range of vision and passing ability. Then Rogers took the ball up the pitch in broken-up play and made things happen.

But those two have gone. If you were Unai Emery and asking who would you sell, Tielemans and Rogers would have been the last two.

And if I was a Villa fan applying for a season ticket, I'd make sure those two players were there first. Because you want to be entertained. And they are entertaining.

And I think Ezri Konsa could go as well. Arsenal might go for him, and Chelsea might buy him too. They need a centre-back.

Johan Manzambi looks alright. But he's just alright. When you look at these players when they come in, you have to ask: who else is after them?

Image: Morgan Rogers played 45 per cent of his minutes last season as a left winger

It's the same with Arsenal signing Christos Tzolis. He might be a wonderkid, but they weren't batting elite clubs away to get him. Were Real Madrid, Barcelona, Man City, Man Utd and Liverpool after the likes of Tzolis and Manzambi?

Sports.title: Tuchel's subs, Rodri's rank, Messi's masterclass - World Cup highs & lows
Sports.content:
As the World Cup draws to a close, with Spain crowned champions for the second time in their history, Sky Sports writers reflect on a tournament that captured the world's attention - but also suffered its fair share of controversy.

Arise Sir Rodri, Spain's ultimate superpower

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player With the World Cup now over, which players are the standout contenders to win the Ballon d'Or?

Player of the tournament - Rodri

Spain are not crowned champions without Rodri's poise and control in midfield. If you don't believe me, watch the France semi-final back. A master at work. Across the tournament, he played over 100 more open-play passes than any other player. He only really had his Spanish team-mates for competition. Just all-round genius.

Goal of the tournament - Julian Alvarez vs Switzerland

Julian Alvarez's stunner for Argentina against Switzerland was a wonderful goal in its own right. The distance, the curl, the nestle top right. But to deliver such class in extra-time of a knockout game under such pressure and intensity makes it truly outstanding.

Moment of the tournament - Messi hat-trick vs Algeria

Few UK viewers would have watched this masterclass live because the game kicked off at ridiculous o'clock. But I did. And it was special, proving beyond doubt that he is the greatest. The beautiful game lit up by its most peerless pioneer. Absolutely worth the early alarm.

Game of the tournament - Argentina 3-2 Cape Verde

Obviously Mexico-England was absolute cinema. But for a point of difference, I've gone with Cape Verde running Argentina ragged. The lowest-ranked nation ever to qualify for the knockout stage pushing the reigning champions to the brink was gold.

Breakout star - Pau Cubarsi

Lots of hype about Ayyoub Bouaddi, but I didn't see enough of him to win this category. I loved the contribution of Pau Cubarsi for Spain. At 19, he's already among the world's best in his position. So commanding and positionally intelligent for one so young, and of course he has the Spanish charm offensive in possession, too.

Biggest disappointment - Balogun red card overturned

This had to be addressed somewhere. A complete sham, making a mockery of the game and those who run it. Folarin Balogun's involvement in the USA's last-16 loss to Belgium won't be remembered for the football, but for political interference. They only succeeded in making themselves public enemy number one. What a way to tarnish an otherwise fantastic tournament.

Laura Hunter

Kane still an elite goalscorer - but Tuchel disappointed

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player England captain Harry Kane reflects on England's third place at the World Cup, backs head coach Thomas Tuchel to succeed with England and does not rule out playing one more World Cup

Player of the tournament - Lionel Messi

We have been truly blessed as fans of this great game to witness one final hurrah from the greatest to ever do it.

Goal of the tournament - Harry Kane vs DR Congo

This was Kane in a nutshell and identifies what makes him the elite goalscorer he is. All he needed was half a yard and bang. It has to rank higher due it being a winning goal, too.

Moment of the tournament - Ecuador's win over Germany

For sheer explosion of colour and vibrancy from the Yellow Wall, it had to be Ecuador's winning goal over the heavyweights of Germany to seal a place in the knockouts.

Game of the tournament - Mexico 2-3 England

Having been live blogging football matches for Sky Sports for over 10 years now, I thought I had seen it all. But England winning a knockout match at the Azteca to the backdrop of such carnage and adversity is up there with the best matches I've ever worked on.

Breakout star - Ayyoub Bouaddi

He became only the second 18-year-old to play for Morocco at a World Cup and produced some immaculate displays in central midfield showing a maturity beyond his years.

Biggest disappointment - High-profile managers

Thomas Tuchel, Carlo Ancelotti, Marcelo Bielsa and Mauricio Pochettino all suffered shambolic exits from the competition with a failure to bring their day-to-day body of work to this type of format.

Lewis Jones

Joyous Cape Verde a reminder of what makes World Cup special

Image: Haiti's Wilson Isidor celebrates scoring during the first half of the Group C match against Morocco (AP Photo/Stew Milne)

Player of the tournament - Lionel Messi

Showed exactly why he is the greatest to ever do it. He was instrumental in pushing Argentina all the way to another final, and they always have a chance when he is on the pitch.

Goal of the tournament - Wilson Isidor vs Morocco

The one that immediately came to mind. A brilliant hit from range that curled beautifully into the top corner. Highly recommend a watch if you've not seen it.

Moment of the tournament - Cape Verde reach the round of 32

A goalless draw with Saudi Arabia secured Cape Verde's spot in the round of 32, setting up a blockbuster tie with Argentina - which they were not far off winning. The celebrations were joyous and offered a timely reminder of why the World Cup is so special.

Game of the tournament - Mexico 2-3 England

A game that had everything - intense build-up, history, weather delays, goals and drama. England's best overall performance and a game that will go down as one of the best ever at a World Cup.

Breakout star - Elliot Anderson

While he was well-known to Premier League fans, Anderson has cemented himself as a solid international midfielder. He was not perfect in every game, but showed his quality.

Biggest disappointment - Uruguay

A disaster from start to finish. From Marcelo Bielsa's refusal to look at the camera during pre-tournament media, to crashing out at the group stage with just two points from three games after draws against Cape Verde and Saudi Arabia. It wasn't even enough to go through as one of the best third-place teams.

Charlotte Marsh

Breakout Bouaddi shines in shop window

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player With Rodri linked with a move away from Manchester City, Sky Sports News reporter Ben Ransom discusses whether Ayyoub Bouaddi could be brought in to replace the midfielder

Player of the tournament - Lionel Messi

Just the GOAT doing GOAT things. If this is the end for Messi on the international stage, what a final chapter.

Goal of the tournament - Julian Alvarez vs Switzerland

The finish is one thing. The fact it came in the second half of extra-time where Alvarez's energy would've been spent is another. One word: unbelievable.

Moment of the tournament - Messi's hat-trick vs Algeria

This has been a World Cup where all the big stars have shown up and showed out. Nothing epitomises that quite like Lionel Messi bagging a hat-trick against Algeria in Argentina's opener. It set the tone for the tournament and began an incredible battle between him and Kylian Mbappe for the golden boot.

Game of the tournament - Mexico 2-3 England

All the odds were stacked against England. In a different era, the players would've collapsed under the pressure. Not in this era.

Breakout star - Ayyoub Bouaddi

This was a tournament where those at the twilight of their careers took centre stage. However, one man who ensured that people saw him as one for the future was Ayyoub Bouaddi. The teenager held down the midfield for a very competitive Morocco and put himself in the shop window with European giants circling.

Biggest disappointment - Brazil

The hype around Neymar's return. Don Carlo Ancelotti at the helm. Yet Brazil looked like the furthest thing from Brazil throughout the tournament. Aside from a comfortable win over Scotland, they never looked like they had the balance in the squad right and they were made to pay.

Callum Bishop

Messi the GOAT leaves World Cup legacy unlike any other

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Jay Bothroyd debates why he thinks Lionel Messi's x-factor means he should have won player of the tournament at the World Cup over Spain's Rodri

Player of the tournament - Lionel Messi

No question, it has to be the GOAT. No player has played (34) or won (23) more World Cup games than him. No one has scored more goals than him (21) or scored in as many matches as him (16). His contributions against England were crucial. If this is to be his last World Cup, what a legacy he leaves.

Goal of the tournament - Sidny Lopes Cabral vs Argentina

If World Cup debutants Cape Verde taking the reigning world champions to extra-time was not enough, Cabral produced a moment of magic that almost forced penalties. He cut in off the left, effortlessly dragged the ball past Alexis Mac Allister, tip-toed into the box and bent a beauty into the top-right corner.

Moment of the tournament - Cape Verde reach knockouts

Bubista's side were written off before the first ball had been kicked, but naysayers were soon forced to swallow their words. The Blue Sharks not only qualified for the knockout stages, but did so after holding both Spain and Uruguay. With spirit and heart in abundance, they shocked the world - and they will be back.

Game of the tournament - Mexico 2-3 England

There are a handful of contenders in this category, but England's win in the Azteca simply has to take it. All the talk beforehand was about whether the Three Lions could handle the altitude; they did that and then some.

Breakout star - Johan Manzambi

Last season's Europa League Young Player of the Year announced himself to the world with Switzerland's opener against Bosnia-Herzegovina just 166 seconds after his introduction. He added a second later on, a goal and an assist against Canada, then another assist against Algeria in the last 32. Injury prevented him playing again, but he left a lasting impression and will shine at Aston Villa.

Biggest disappointment - Cristiano Ronaldo

He would have wanted to go out with a bang, but the reality was far from that. Roberto Martinez persisted with his captain despite pressure to drop him given how ineffective he was on the whole. He did score three goals - two against Uzbekistan, one against Croatia - Messi's success will have irked him.

Dan Long

Tuchel cost England a World Cup final

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Thomas Tuchel hits back at the negativity around England following their World Cup semi-final exit to Argentina saying it felt like they had gone out of the group stges without a win...

Player of the tournament - Lionel Messi

Still delivering at 39 years old. What else is there to say? The best ever.

Goal of the tournament - Sidny Lopes Cabral vs Argentina

Not only the goal of the tournament but the celebration too. Cape Verde's dream run hit new heights when Sidny Lopes Cabral curled a stunning equaliser into the top right corner during extra-time before ending up in the crowd celebrating with his loved ones.

Moment of the tournament - Dan Burn blocking Raul Jimenez's overhead kick

Big Dan Burn put his head in where it hurts to deliver a moment that will go down in English football history, not only blocking Raul Jimenez's audacious overhead kick, but sending the ball all the way into the Mexico half without bouncing.

Game of the tournament - Mexico 2-3 England

An absolute all-timer that lived up to its billing. The Azteca. The 2am kick-off. Jude Bellingham's 98-second double. Jarell Quansah's red card. Harry Kane's penalty. England's defensive grit. It had everything.

Breakout star - Johan Manzambi

Not starting the 20-year-old in the 1-1 draw against Qatar was the only misstep for Switzerland at their best-ever World Cup. Manzambi then scored twice against Bosnia-Herzegovina and added another plus two assists in two more matches. A real shame that injury cut short his tournament.

Biggest disappointment - Tuchel's substitutions vs Argentina

"They were more afraid to drop out of the tournament, in my observation, than having the excitement and hunger to win it," Thomas Tuchel said of England's Euro 2024 campaign. How ironic. Ezri Konsa coming for goalscorer Anthony Gordon in the 72nd minute showed just how little had changed under Tuchel.

David Richardson

USA scored biggest own goal in tournament history after Balogun sham decision

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Geraint Hughes explains what could happen next in Folarin Balogun's red card controversy, despite Belgium beating the USA in the World Cup

Player of the tournament - Lionel Messi

Nothing more needs said. The greatest to ever do it.

Goal of the tournament - Sidny Lopes Cabral vs Argentina

There's a few contenders for best strike but you're not giving this one to a Giovanni Reyna fourth against Paraguay. Cabral's finish was magnificent and so was the story around it. Cape Verde are everything the World Cup is about. So was the celebration.

Moment of the tournament - Vozinha's interview

Not to make this a Cape Verde fan entry but a 40-year-old goalkeeper, who plays for a second-tier club in Portugal, crying in front of hundreds of millions of people and wishing his mum could've been there to watch him. In a world of miserable news, we need more of these moments.

Game of the tournament - Mexico 2-3 England

It had everything. The Azteca. Lightning delays. VAR controversy. A red card. Five goals. A historic win. And one heck of a defensive unit for those last 20 minutes.

Breakout star - Pau Cubarsi

The 19-year-old looks like he's been sweeping up at the back for Spain for years. Worth remembering the semi-final win over France was only his 19th cap, and he had won only 12 before this tournament. His stats have ranked among the tournament's best despite his tender years both with and without the ball. A star of the present.

Biggest disappointment - USA

The USA began the tournament without a huge amount of goodwill from elsewhere for a variety of reasons but slowly began to melt hearts around the globe with a likeable team coached by a likeable manager, playing good - and successful - football.

After doubling their knockout wins it looked as though this could be their breakout tournament until Donald Trump's intervention on Folarin Balogun's red card, FIFA's capitulation and then their own collapse under the scrutiny to exit with a whimper against Belgium and any overseas goodwill evaporated, rightly or wrongly.

Ron Walker

Sports.title: What would a 64-team World Cup look like - and could it work in 2030?
Sports.content:
This year's World Cup is finally over - and after 48 teams took part, it was a long, long tournament. But just as we bid to say goodbye to the 2026 edition, this competition may be getting even bigger.

FIFA president Gianni Infantino says any further expansion of the World Cup for 2030 - where six countries are set to host the tournament - ‌will be discussed now the 2026 World Cup has finished.

South American nations Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay - who are set to host one game each before the tournament transfers to main co-hosts Spain, Portugal and Morocco - are calling to host more games.

And one solution FIFA are discussing is a 64-team tournament. More teams, more matches, more talking points.

So if the 2030 World Cup celebrates its centenary year by having 16 more teams than we had this summer, what would that look like?

A six-week tournament!

Image: Fans would have to plan for a six-week World Cup tournament if it rises to 64 teams

A 64-team World Cup would create one heck of a group stage. There would have to be 16 groups of four teams, as 64 does not evenly divide into three. That means group stages would go up from 72 matches to 96.

The 48-team tournament saw those 72 matches played during an intense 16-day period - averaging 4.5 matches a day. If FIFA try to average 4.5 matches a day in a 64-team group stage, then the first part of the tournament would take three weeks.

Given the round of 32 onwards in this World Cup needs another three weeks to complete, that would mean a six-week tournament.

And assuming there is a couple of weeks of pre-tournament preparations for each country, then the 1,664 players taking part in the World Cup would have to give up two months for the competition.

More goals than ever before?

Of course, more games will set new records for most goals in a tournament. The move from the regular 64 games to 104 matches in 2026 set new records. There were 308 goals in this year's World Cup, compared to 172 four years ago.

But what was interesting about the 2026 World Cup is goals flew in at a higher rate per game. There was an average of 2.96 goals per game this year, compared to around 2.6 across the last three tournaments.

One of the reasons for more goals at this World Cup is a greater disparity between the best and worst teams. There was a bigger average gap between teams at this World Cup in terms of the FIFA world rankings than ever seen before.

No more third-placed drama

A 64-team tournament allows for one very simple thing: the third-placed qualification route to the knockout rounds will have to be scrapped.

The only way you can make a round of 32 in this format is by having the top two teams from all 16 groups qualify for the latter stages.

So the rogue calculations about how much goal difference Scotland need to qualify as a third-placed team would likely have to go.

Image: If Scotland qualify for a 64-team World Cup in 2030, it could make their knockout chances a lot harder

However, if the top two teams are the only ones in the group that qualify, it would go back to the 32-team World Cup format where a lot of the final round of group matches were 'dead rubber' occasions between teams already qualified for the next stage, or teams already eliminated.

FIFA would probably have to put goal difference back above head-to-head record in a 64-team tournament to create enough jeopardy in the third and final round of group matches.

Goodbye to the 'one nation host'?

If this becomes a long-term plan from FIFA, a 64-team tournament would effectively confirm that the World Cup can no longer be held by one individual nation.

For the current 48-team tournament, 15 stadia are being used for 12 groups and 104 games. Using those numbers as a template, a move to 64 teams would mean 20 grounds would be needed for 128 matches.

So if England were to host the tournament, nearly the entire Premier League would have to give up their stadium for the summer, assuming Wembley will host matches too. Imagine Brazil playing in Bournemouth…

True, having multiple host nations are the way forward in international football. The 2028 European Championships are across the entire UK and Ireland. Six countries will host the 2030 World Cup. The 2032 European Championships are in Italy and Turkey.

But Saudi Arabia are the sole host for the 2034 FIFA World Cup, and when a 48-team World Cup was considered for the Qatar World Cup in 2022, it was impossible for the Gulf nation to stage such a tournament.

Logistically, there are question marks if 64 teams is the way forward in the long-term.

Who would qualify for a 64-team World Cup?

A 64-team World Cup would mean 30 per cent of all FIFA nations would qualify for the World Cup. But how would the allocations be split?

With a third of the 48 teams, Europe have the largest allocation of qualification spots in the current tournament system. Applying the same logic would mean 21 European countries would take part in a 64-team tournament. Maybe Italy would even qualify…

The vast majority of all confederations would get more spots in the World Cup, if we use the current model as an example.

Sports.title: 'Nothing to blame them for' - Argentina papers defend team after dismal final and brawl
Sports.content:
Argentina's national media defended their team's performance in the World Cup final - despite a defensive and ill-disciplined display.

Lionel Messi's side barely made the game with Spain a contest. They did not have a shot in normal time - nor an effort on target in the entire 120 minutes.

Meanwhile, their ill-discipline came through as Enzo Fernandez was shown two yellow cards - first for dissent, then for a wild clumsy challenge on Pau Cubarsi.

At full-time, Leandro Paredes, who arguably should have joined Fernandez in being sent off for two yellow cards, was given his marching orders for his angry response at the whistle. Nahuel Molina also squared up to Spain players in disgraceful scenes.

"I love the competitiveness of the Argentines but Paredes has been a disgrace the last couple of games," said Gary Neville on commentary for ITV.

However, the Argentina front pages on Monday morning called for national pride despite the 1-0 final loss.

Clarin went for a tearful picture of Messi with the headline. "They gave it their all, nothing to blame them for."

La Nacion went for a similar theme, going with the line: "Argentina gave it their all - and they're a source of national pride."

Another paper Ole went with the headline: "May they be eternal" with another tearful Messi image.

'The world is ours' - Spain react to second World Cup triumph

Spain's front pages, meanwhile, were full of joy as they celebrated their second World Cup triumph.

AS went for the headline "The world is ours" - adding that the win came through "absolute justice".

On El Periodico's front page were the words: "The world surrenders to Spain", while ABC called Spain "invincible" - noting their 38-game unbeaten run in international football.

El Mundo said Spain are "on top of the world" - while multiple papers called Spain "double champions" and "superstars".

Sports.title: Hull KR's Lewis handed four-game ban
Sports.content:
Hull KR star Mikey Lewis has been served with a four-game ban for a late tackle and a headbutt in a 34-12 defeat against Warrington Wolves on Saturday.

Lewis was sin-binned for a tackle on Ewan Irwin during the match, but the scrum-half also appeared to have headbutted Warrington's Adam Holroyd in an incident that was missed by match officials.

The Match Review Panel announced on Monday that it has handed Lewis a one-game ban for a Grade C late-contact penalty for the tackle, while also retrospectively banning him for three extra games for the Grade E-listed headbutt.

Image: Mikey Lewis scored a hat-trick of tries for Hull KR as they got off to a flying start against Wigan Warriors

Image: Picture by Allan McKenzie/SWpix.com - 19/02/2026 - Rugby League - World Club Challenge - Hull KR v Brisbane Broncos - MKM Stadium, Kingston upon Hull, England - Mikey Lewis after victory over Brisbane.

The ban comes after the reigning champions dropped out of the playoff places with their latest defeat, sitting two points behind St Helens Saints with eight games to go in the Super League season.

The Rovers star is now set to miss the Hull derby, as well as fixtures against Bradford Bulls, Castleford Tigers, and Catalans Dragons.

Sports.title: World Cup 2026: Spain’s champions land in Madrid for heroes’ welcome after beating Argentina – live
Sports.content:
2m ago 09.02 EDT The Spain squad have posed for a photograph together on the tarmac … View image in fullscreen The Spain squad in Madrid. Photograph: Pablo Blázquez Domínguez/Getty Images … and with that I will hand you to Daniel Harris. I think this is my last stint on the World Cup news blog until 2030 (the year, not 8.30pm tonight), so until then, take care, thanks for reading, and thanks for all your BTL comments. Adiós! Share

7m ago 08.56 EDT I guess the trophy went via “carry on” luggage then. I hope Rodri has done his customs paperwork. View image in fullscreen Spain's captain Rodri holds up their trophy. Photograph: Óscar del Pozo/AFP/Getty Images Share

9m ago 08.54 EDT Madrid mayor says city is readying to 'celebrate and greet a team that will live for ever in our memory' Sam Jones Sam Jones is in Madrid for the Guardian Madrid’s mayor, José Luis Martínez Almeida, told Radio Nacional de España that the capital was working to give the team the homecoming they deserved. He also hailed the peaceful and joyous scenes that had greeted Spain’s victory. “Even though there were thousands and thousands of people on the streets last night, there were practically no incidents in the city,” he said. “We’re getting everything ready for tonight and the musical events should starts at Cibeles from about 6pm, with the parade scheduled to start at 7pm – but all this is depends on various factors … The thing we’re focusing on is how to celebrate and greet a team that will live for ever in our memory.” View image in fullscreen Fans of Spain on the streets of Madrid last night. Photograph: Xinhua/Shutterstock Share

11m ago 08.52 EDT Spain team expected to meet King Felipe after arriving in Madrid Sam Jones Sam Jones is in Madrid for the Guardian The team have a busy afternoon and a long night ahead of them. Their first official stop is expected to be the Zarzuela palace outside Madrid, where they will be greeted by King Felipe and Queen Letizia at about 4.30pm. After that, they’re due to head to the Moncloa palace – the office and residence of the prime minister – for 6pm The PM, Pedro Sánchez, is presently on a trip to Algeria, but may hotfoot it back to Madrid to welcome the squad. After that, the victory parade kicks off in earnest, and will travel from Moncloa into town at around 7pm. The focus of the festivities will be the Plaza de Cibeles just outside Madrid city hall. Expect music, massive crowds – and another busy few hours for Madrid’s tireless municipal street cleaners. View image in fullscreen Rodri of Spain lifts the trophy alongside Luis de la Fuente in Madrid. Photograph: Pablo Blázquez Domínguez/Getty Images Share

15m ago 08.49 EDT Judging by the photos dropping from Madrid on the wires it looks like the plane carrying the team got a quick paint/decal job overnight … View image in fullscreen A picture of Spain players is seen on the team plane as they arrive at Madrid Airport. Photograph: Violeta Santos Moura/Reuters Share

18m ago 08.46 EDT Victorious Spain team land in Madrid for heroes' welcome Spain’s winning World Cup team has landed in Madrid, with tens of thousands of fans expected to greet them during the course of the day. Less than 24 hours after lifting the trophy in the New York New Jersey stadium, Spain’s squad are back home. The Iberia aircraft carrying the squad touched down at Madrid-Barajas airport at 14:30 local time under clear blue skies. View image in fullscreen Spain players return to Madrid after winning the World Cup. Photograph: Violeta Santos Moura/Reuters Share Updated at 08.48 EDT

31m ago 08.33 EDT Sam Jones Sam Jones is in Madrid for the Guardian It’s fair to say that Madrid – and the rest of Spain - is quite excited by the prospect of the team’s imminent return. La Roja is due to touch down at Adolfo Suárez Madrid-Barajas Airport in around 10 minutes. According to El País, the first of many heroes’ welcomes is already massing at the airport, which sits at the northeastern edge of the capital. double quotation mark Between 200 and 300 fans are already waiting at Terminal 4 of the airport to welcome the Spanish national team after their World Cup victory. Families with children, groups of friends, and supporters who have traveled from all over the country are lining up in a makeshift corridor, wearing Spanish jerseys, waving flags around their necks, and using their mobile phones, hoping to catch a glimpse of Luis de la Fuente’s team. The Edinburgh side, under the tutelage of new head coach Wouter Vrancken, will face the Austrians in the first leg of their second qualifier on Tuesday before the second leg at Tynecastle next week. 3h ago 06.30 EDT I watched both channels because I was paid to do so. It was a finely balanced thing between the two broadcasters. I think ITV missed a trick by sticking with their main show being hosted from the Brooklyn studio when they could have been at the stadium. Equally, I thought their commentary was more enjoyable amid a pretty dreadful game. BBC’s trio of guests seemed a bit livelier and very happy to be in attendance, while Roy Keane and chums felt less engaged. Most people select the BBC purely to avoid the adverts and on this occasion, they would have been right to do so. ITV, as is their business model, had ads straight after the half-time whistle which lasted for a while, resulting in the briefest of punditry chats before the awful 'show’ was played in full. Share

This means BBC has increased its viewership from four years ago when 9.2m saw the 2022 final with Gary Lineker et al, compared to 2.8m on ITV. The peak audience on BBC was 13.6m vs ITV’s 3.4m.
