The Imalu Tigers had not yet won the flag, but their devoted supporters never gave them a reason to doubt their hopes of securing back-to-back premiership glory.

Some Tigers fans were so passionate, they ran onto the field each time their team scored. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

For the thousands of people living on the Tiwi Islands, Aussie Rules is much more than a friendly sport. It's a religion, and it all culminates on grand final day.

And for the many visitors attending the grand final game at Wurrumiyanga Oval on Bathurst Island, about 80 kilometres north of Darwin, it is a once-in-a-lifetime experience.

Tapalinga Super Stars players and supporters hug after their win in the women's grand final match. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

Each year, hundreds of tourists charter planes and catch ferries across to the Tiwi Islands to watch some of Australia's most promising upcoming AFL players battle it out in front of their home crowds.

This year, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese was one of them, becoming the first Australian leader to attend the game while in office.

The Tigers' opponents, the Ranku Eagles, also had plenty of supporters. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

Victory for Imalu Tigers, Tapalinga Super Stars

Despite the opposing team, the Ranku Eagles, having the home-ground advantage, Melville Island's Imalu Tigers had the real upper hand, with droves of loyal supporters dominating the fence lines.

With reigning premiers Imalu only having lost a single game this season, it was always going to be a David-and-Goliath battle.

The men's grand final game was close early on before the Tigers pulled away. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

At half-time, it appeared the Eagles stood a chance, with the Tigers only narrowly in front by 12 points.

But in the third quarter, Imalu doubled their lead and soon became unstoppable.

For the second time in as many years, the Tigers took home the premiership cup, claiming victory in a thrilling 11.9 (75) to 7.8 (50) win against Ranku.

The winning Tigers team lifts the cup. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

One young Tigers fan told the ABC he hopes to be playing alongside his male relatives next season.

"It's the sport we grew up with and we just love playing it," he said.

"We love to beat people in it. It can get a bit rough, but yeah, we love it."

The Imalu Tigers had a dominant season in the lead-up to the final. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

In the women's division, it was a tight contest until the end between the Tapalinga Super Stars and the Jikilarruwu.

It was tit-for-tat for much of the first half of the game between the two sides, before Tapalinga created some distance in the third quarter, leaving Jikilarruwu trailing by 10 points.

As the final siren sounded, cheers were met with tears as the Super Stars won the game, defeating Jikilarruwu Thunder & Lightning 8.9 (57) to 4.8 (32).

Player with the Tapalinga Super Stars pose with the premiership cup. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

Huge day of art trade

Grand final day is the largest social event on the Tiwi Islands' social calendar, attracting hundreds of tourists to the community from around the country.

With art centres open amid the influx of visitors, for the islands' artists, the event also doubles as their biggest day of trade and an opportunity to pour money back into the local economy.

Artist Romolo Kantilla said it was also an important time to share their culture.

Romolo Kantilla says the grand final is an opportunity for Tiwi Islands people to share their culture through art. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

"It's a very special day for Tiwi people, it's a big day and we get everyone from the mainland and it's a good time to come see the art," he said.

"The art is based on creation stories, totem and country.

"Art is always part of us Tiwi people."

World.title: Breakthrough win for Bernard Tomic after lean tennis times
World.content:
Bernard Tomic is back in the winner's circle with the Australian veteran cracking his first Challenger Tour title in eight years.

Reaching the final of the Lincoln Challenger tournament in Nebraska, the 33-year-old showed some grit to save a championship point before downing Estonian Mark Lajal 4-6, 7-6 (4), 7-6 (3).

With a world ranking of 206, down from a career-high of number 17 back in 2016, Tomic started as the underdog against 23-year-old Lajal, who is ranked world number 159.

The crafty Queenslander nailed his service games, on target with 72 per cent of first serves as well as nine aces to cause headaches for his rival.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Tomic also had a three-set battle to book his place in the final, downing American wildcard Spencer Johnson 6-7 (5), 6-3, 6-2.

It was his fourth Challenger Tour title, with the last coming in Mallorca in Spain in 2018.

A quarter-finalist at Wimbledon back in 2011 and former junior champion, Tomic recently lost in the second round of qualifying, falling to fellow Australian Chris O'Connell 6-4, 6-4.

On the main ATP Tour, his most recent singles title was at the ATP 250 event in Chengdu in 2018.

AAP

World.title: Spain's World Cup win a reminder collective spirit trumps solo stars
World.content:
You could see it in the Spanish players as they floated euphorically, each kissing the top of the trophy.

You could feel it from the fans in the stands as they straddled that blurry line between overwhelmed and overjoyed.

And you could hear it rumble through Spain, as a nation united through something which in reality should not mean this much but means more than almost anything else.

Nick Hornby summed it up best in his classic football-themed memoir Fever Pitch.

"I fell in love with football as I was later to fall in love with women: suddenly, inexplicably, uncritically, giving no thought to the pain or disruption it would bring with it."

Argentina felt its force too, the scenes of Lionel Messi in tears, fans distraught, Leandro Paredes losing control and lashing out.

Lionel Messi was crushed after the defeat. (Getty Images: Michael Regan)

In that moment they thought may a love like this never find me.

World Cup football can twist and torment, ripping out your heart and stamping on it till you feel like it can never be repaired.

It can also make you fall head over heels and erase all the hurt you ever felt before.

La Roja ruthless in victory

Spain captain Rodri takes in the magnitude of the achievement. (Getty Images: Alex Pantling )

Spain coach Luis de la Fuente spoke about it in his own terms before the semi-final against France, drawing on inspiration from Julius Caesar, and the idea of having to suffer to achieve great things.

And this was a game that was a struggle for all, it lacked the overall quality and excitement you might expect from a final.

Argentina was stubborn and produced heroic defending in the box, but again questionable roughhousing tactics, eventually resulting in Enzo Fernández's send off.

The reigning champions showed little initiative to create much of anything until the final minutes of extra time as their dream dissipated in the warm New Jersey air.

Spain, having only conceded one goal all tournament, and with 20 shots to two in the decider, might not have produced its flashiest performance, but it was its most important.

This is what La Roja has done throughout the past six weeks, control the ball effortlessly, win it back almost immediately, build pressure through well-organised and committed structures, and wait till late to put it all to bed.

Ferran Torres celebrates the goal that proved to be the decider in the World Cup final between Argentina and Spain. (Getty Images)

The Spaniards were particularly effective in shutting out Messi, who saw little of the ball and was quickly dispossessed or forced into errors when he did have it.

Turns out he can be stopped; it just takes the most exceptional defensive team of this tournament to do it.

The European Champions are now World Champions for the second time, unbeaten for 38 straight matches, a magnificent footballing dynasty growing with every game, becoming the first country to simultaneously hold the men's and women's World Cups.

"I'm so proud of this generation of footballers who have grown up with this philosophy, remained true to it, made it even better and set an example as a team and a family," Spain coach Luis de la Fuente said.

"They're excellent, world-class footballers with exceptional talent. I'm very moved. Looking back and thinking about them, we've won everything, absolutely everything, with this generation of players."

Spain's collective triumph

Celebrations in Madrid will continue long after tonight. (Getty Images: Chris McGrath)

Argentina is a team built around one player, the likes of whom we have never seen before.

Spain is built around a collective approach, filled with exceptional players, but all who work in harmony, allowing each other to shine in different moments.

Like Mikel Merino with his repeated winners off the bench, or Rodri holding the side together as the linchpin in midfield, or Ferran Torres with his vital assists, and today's match-winning strike.

"I think in the end the goal came from 47 million people, not just those of us that are here," Torres said.

"Today destiny was written, it was made for us to win. We're far from our people today but we tried to be as close as possible to them.

"A huge relief [to score]. I've been criticised throughout the whole tournament but as I said before, destiny was written."

It says so much that Lamine Yamal, 19, seen by most as Messi's heir, did not play much of an influential role in this final, or at any stage during the tournament.

Lamine Yamal did not quite have the breakout tournament some predicted. (Getty Images: Evrim Aydin/Anadolu)

He was not a passenger, but was certainly not a conductor, and that can only breed even further confidence, and strike further fear into other nations, as he goes from boy to man.

This World Cup started slowly for Spain, a scoreless draw with the tournament's best underdog story, Cabo Verde.

But as the superstars like Messi, Kylian Mbappé, Erling Haaland, Harry Kane, and Jude Bellingham took all the headlines and dominated social media algorithms, Spain was the quiet, conscientious achiever.

That all changed with the terrifyingly efficient dismantling of France in the semifinals, and now a completely deserved win in the final.

"This generation of players is an example for Spanish sport, for the Spanish youth," de la Fuente said.

"Together we are much stronger, and that is why we don't forget anyone."

A team forged through fire, built on discipline and togetherness, now enjoying its love story.

World.title: Tears streaming down his face, Messi leaves the World Cup stage a legend
World.content:
Lionel Messi had so desperately hoped his World Cup would end differently.

Tears running down his cheeks, a silver medal around his neck, his teammates in various states of depression, strewn around him like the detritus of some cataclysmic event as Spain roared amid garish golden confetti and an explosion of colour and joy.

Arguably the greatest player to ever grace a pitch was distraught.

It's impossible to know exactly what was going through his mind.

A decade earlier, on the same Metlife Stadium pitch where he was currently sobbing, Messi had tearfully decided to retire from international football after losing the Copa América final against enormous underdogs Chile.

The pain of that defeat was simply too much to bear for Messi, saddled with the expectation of a nation desperate to anoint him as Maradona's heir.

The world was the beneficiary as Messi reversed that decision.

Fans around the world have rejoiced at Messi's success. (Getty Images: Wang HE)

So too were Argentina, who claimed the 2021 Copa América title, the 2022 Finalissima and, most tellingly, the 2022 World Cup under Messi's leadership, cementing his legacy among his fellow countrymen for all time.

But once again in the New Jersey sunshine, Messi's tears were the defining feature for a generation of football fans.

Was this another tearful goodbye to the international stage?

Messi is 39 years old.

With 19-year-olds Lamine Yamal and Pau Cubarsí on the other side of the divide and winning for Spain, the next generation is not just arriving to force him out but has already arrived.

To play another World Cup in four years may be beyond even his mystic powers, even despite his impressive ability to adapt to the constraints his age has imposed on him.

The next generation, personified by Lamine Yamal, is snapping at Messi's aging heels. (Getty Images: PA Images/Bradley Collyer)

At this World Cup, Messi has walked for roughly half the time he was on the pitch, strolling and stalking for about 5 kilometres per game.

And yet, inarguably, no one player has had a greater role in his team's success than Messi has for Argentina.

His goals, eight of them, and his four assists dragged the defending champions through the group stage and the knockout rounds.

His ability to bend a game to his will, no matter the situation, made him seem nothing short of inevitable.

Despite all the walking, whenever Argentina threatened, the little magician was there in the heart of the action, conjuring and scheming and dragging his team home just when they needed him to.

His very presence seemed to inspire his teammates to feats beyond their capabilities, a totemic figure to rally around, his energy imbuing those around him with positivity and confidence and class.

Lionel Messi came close to lifting the World Cup for the second time. (Getty Images: FIFA/Tullio Puglia)

Against England in the semifinal, his two assists powered the Albiceleste to a famous victory in stoppage time.

Against Egypt, as his team faced elimination at 2-0 down, he provided the cross for the first and delivered the shot for its equaliser.

Against Spain in the final? It just didn't happen.

The fact that his tears only came after he had been given his silver medal was almost illustrative: No matter how late it got, Messi perhaps still had hope that he might somehow manage to influence the game in his favour.

He'd done it before, after all.

Only when Donald Trump laid the heavy silver slice of defeat around his neck did he realise there would be no more magic, that no amount of sorcery from his phenomenal feet could change history now.

Against Spain, the little master managed just 55 touches, none of which came in the Spain penalty area.

Lionel Messi was unable to stamp his authority on the contest. (Getty Images: FIFA/Maja Hitij)

He was stifled as effectively as if Spain wrapped him in a blanket.

And his Argentina teammates simply couldn't back up their superstar when it mattered most.

Messi could not deliver the magical moment that his nation demanded.

It was telling that Argentina offered so little other than niggly fouls and angry words as opposed to the free-flowing football Spain occasionally managed when the mood took them.

Let's not beat around the bush: Argentina were woeful in this final.

Argentina didn't have a single shot on goal in the first 90 minutes of the game, the first time any team has failed to do so in a World Cup final.

Their first attempt on goal did not come until the 26th minute of extra time.

Lionel Messi had Argentina's first shot of the game, in the second half of extra time. (Getty Images: FIFA/Maja Hitij)

Their 25 total fouls resulted in seven yellow cards, one of which was a second that saw Enzo Fernández up-end Pau Cubarsí, making him the sixth player ever to be dismissed in a World Cup final.

Argentina's nefarious skulduggery was finally, belatedly, penalised by a referee brave enough not to stand for it.

Coach Lionel Scaloni said afterwards that his team "showed that we know how to lose" in his post-match press conference, but nothing could be further from the truth.

The Argentines thoroughly disgraced themselves after the game's conclusion, Leandro Paredes lashing out and sparking a minor brawl that ended with him shown a red card after the final whistle.

Fractious barely covers it.

If this is to be his international swan song, the landscape post-Messi may as well be post-apocalyptic, so absent of joy and light does it appear to hold.

Claudio Tapia, the president of the Argentina Football Association, knows how important Messi is to the team. (Getty Images: Andrew Harnik)

It was not Messi's fault that he could not have the impact on the game he might have hoped for.

Spain were able to successfully nullify a far better team than Argentina in the semifinal with their Rodri-led midfield dominance suffocating their opponents' creativity.

Messi simply didn't have the space.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

He was closed down as ominously and relentlessly as the ticking of the clock that will one day herald the end of his stellar career.

Messi couldn't muster the magic to help Argentina become the third men's team to win back-to-back World Cups.

It is not the finale that Messi might have envisaged.

But if this is to be his tearful sign off, fans will still look back at having been blessed by one of football's greatest of all time.

World.title: The 13 photos that summed up the chaos of the 2026 World Cup final
World.content:
It was a tournament where the football was magical, the off-field antics were questionable, and ultimately, Spain left the United States as the champions of the world.

A day after the utter chaos of the third-placed playoff between France and England, where 10 goals were scored, Argentina and Spain played things a little more conservatively — right up until the game exploded into action.

Here are the 13 photos that tell the story of the 2026 FIFA World Cup final.

1. The Fresh Prince of Barcelona

Teenage superstar Lamine Yamal arrives at the stadium looking like the coolest dude on earth. (Getty Images: Evrim Aydin/Anadolu)

While much of the tournament had been focused on the more established superstar names like Lionel Messi, Erling Haaland and Kylian Mbappé, teenager Lamine Yamal had floated under the radar for the World Cup passers-by.

Coming to the final having never lost a match where he had started for Spain, expectations were high on the 19-year-old as he came into the stadium. Would he be the hero Spain needed to overcome the perceived might of Argentina?

Whatever the pressure, he arrived looking like the coolest dude on the planet; calm, collected and rocking a style straight out of The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air.

2. Smoke and mirrors

Mark Carney greets Donald Trump ahead of the World Cup final. (Getty Images: Eva Marie Uzcategui)

All eyes turned to the skies before kick-off as US President Donald Trump made his usual subtle entrance into the arena, coming in low and fast in the Marine One helicopter.

Once settled in prime position in a corporate box on the wings, Trump was afforded the questionable chance to give the trophy a little pat as FIFA boss Gianni Infantino brought the iconic gold statue to Trump's seat.

Before that, though, there was the potentially awkward meeting between Trump and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, just a couple of days after Trump accused Canada of being "filthy" and "polluted" over its wildfire smoke that had blanketed New York in the lead-up to the tournament.

All-in-all, things seemed reasonably diplomatic, given Mother Nature had done her job to send the smoke packing just in time for the game.

3. America makes a double Buff

American announcer Bruce Buffer turns the World Cup into a blood sport briefly with his iconic introduction. (Getty Images: Sebastian Widmann)

In the most American moment of this entire game, event organisers decided that what this little old soccer match needed was a double Buffer.

Bruce and Michael Buffer, to be exact, the legendary ring announcers from every blood sport imaginable.

Flipping from one brother to the next, the pair excitedly announced that the game was "ready to rumble", in scenes not far off that time that soccer came to Springfield in The Simpsons.

4. The GOAT meets the rising star

Lionel Messi and Lamine Yamal share a laugh together early in the match. (Getty Images: Hannah Peters)

Looking a little less cool than when he arrived, but still the picture of confidence, Yamal made a beeline for Lionel Messi before the match to wish arguably the greatest player in history some luck.

It was a full-circle moment for the pair, who originally met on a photo shoot in 2007 when Yamal's parents won a UNICEF raffle to have Yamal photographed for a calendar with the then rising star Messi.

This time around, Messi's hair was a little shorter and his face a little more wearied, while Yamal was a little less nude.

5. The World Cup's Mariah Carey

Shakira performs during the half-time show, a spectacle one England footballing legend would go on to call "crap". (Getty Images: Lars Baron)

Shakira was rolled out for the half-time show, with the Colombian star fast becoming to the World Cup what Mariah Carey is to Christmas.

She's just always there.

While her performance was fantastic, the rest of it — from Justin Bieber to Madonna to BTS — left a little bit to be desired.

So much so that English footballing champion Wayne Rooney didn't hold back with what he thought.

"I thought it was crap," he said on the BBC coverage.

6. The spectacular red card

Enzo Fernandez fouls Spain's Pau Cubarsi, leading to the Argentinian's second yellow card and a send-off. (Getty Images: Al Bello)

As soon as we all saw it happen on the TV, we knew that the photos were going to be spectacular.

And veteran Getty photographer Al Bello didn't let us down.

Rising Spanish star Pau Cubarsí was sent flying by Argentina's Enzo Fernández, but it was made all the more spectacular by Cubarsí really leaning into the flip.

Had Fernández not already had a yellow, it's unlikely he would have been sent off at all, but the red card made it all the more dramatic as the scores stood at 0-0 heading into the death.

7. Hydration break goes to a new level

Spain's Dani Olmo takes the hydration break to the extreme as he utilises the sprinklers to cool down. (Getty Images: Evrim Aydin/Anadolu)

Two things have been major talking points during this tournament: it's been bloody hot and the hydration breaks have been bloody irritating.

So it was fun to see the two come together in the final regular-time break of the tournament, as the Spanish players took advantage of the sprinklers to cool off.

Was it the trick that won them the World Cup? Who's to say. But almost certainly yes.

8. Free kick wipes a goal

Nico Williams reacts after his goal was marked off for a foul that was immediately obvious on the replays afterwards. (Getty Images: Carl Recine)

In a moment of brilliance, Nico Williams looked to have won it for Spain when he slotted a goal past the keeper to make it 1-0 late.

But the referee called it back. There was a free kick somewhere in the mess of bodies in the box.

In live action it wasn't immediately clear where the free kick was. On replay, it still wasn't totally clear.

But on the fifth or sixth watch: yeah, no idea.

Williams was furious, and rightfully so.

9. Deadlock ends in headlock

Nico Williams gives Ferran Torres a little chokehold celebration after Torres scored the winning goal. (Getty Images: Nick Potts)

Go back to the very first photo at the top of this story and you can experience the majesty of the Ferran Torres goal that broke the game open.

Hair blowing in the breeze, his teammates running in behind him, the fans screaming and cheering in ecstasy.

And then Williams decided to choke Torres for some reason.

Angry that he wasn't the hero after his goal was wiped? An in-joke that we don't know about?

Who knows. But it made for an odd scene in an incredible moment.

10. Tears of a legend

Lionel Messi slumps to the ground after the final whistle, in what will likely be the football legend's last World Cup game. (Getty Images: Michael Regan)

Small in stature but grand in legacy, Messi cut a forlorn figure after the final whistle.

His tiny body huddled in the middle of the massive stadium was enough to make anyone feel sorry for the attacking superstar.

His place as the greatest player the game has ever seen would have been secured had he managed to drag his teammates to victory, but even Messi couldn't get his countrymen through the incredible defensive wall that Spain had built.

11. Infantino chases after Trump

Rodri prepares to lift trophy as Gianni Infantino attempts to move Donald Trump out of frame. (Getty Images: Dan Mullan)

Trump had made headlines this time last year when he joined Chelsea on stage for the celebrations in the Club World Cup final, despite the apparent confusion of the players.

This time there was surely no way that Trump would be caught right in the middle of the pack as the Spanish players lifted the most coveted trophy in world sport, right?

Well, kind of. This time Trump wandered right across stage as Infantino pivoted left, leaving the FIFA boss to scramble after the US president, with the pair awkwardly caught in the team celebration photos.

On the broadcast, you could hear someone say "they'll crop him out" in an unexpected, but funny, hot mic moment.

12. Utter heartache for Argentina

Argentina goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez shows his dejection as the ceremony for the winners gets into full swing. (Getty Images: Ryan Pierse)

Goalkeeper Emiliano Martínez had been immense through the World Cup.

But as Spain lifted the trophy, the Aston Villa keeper let the emotions flow, caught by the camera as he sat on the sidelines thinking about what might have been.

It was a reminder of what this thing, this silly, epic, immense mess of a game, means to the people who play it.

13. The love of a mum

Lamine Yamal's mum races out onto the field to celebrate the victory with her son. (Getty Images: John Todd)

In the end, all we really want is the hug of a mum who's proud of you.

And that's what Yamal got as his mum, Sheila, ran onto the ground to give her son a big old cuddle.

Having given birth at just 16 years old as an immigrant from Equatorial Guinea, Sheila's story is the one that really captures the essence of the World Cup.

Not the championship rings or corporate boxes. Not the powerful men in powerful suits making powerful political moves.

A mum with a dream for her son to shine on the world stage.

This was the moment that really mattered.

World.title: Bombers star cleared for return despite abrupt mid-game hospital visit
World.content:
Essendon's star forward Nate Caddy has been cleared to return to action after being hospitalised with an elevated heart rate.

Caddy was sent to hospital during the Bombers' win against GWS on Sunday but was discharged that night.

The 21-year-old is expected to train with his teammates this week and play against Hawthorn on Saturday.

"There was some concern in the first quarter when Nate's heart rate became elevated," Essendon's football boss Dan McPherson said on Monday.

"He was removed from the game and our medical team assessed him at the ground before sending him to hospital for further assessment.

"He was discharged last night and is back at home."

McPherson said Caddy, who recently signed a contract extension until the end of 2031, was expected to "train and play without concern this week".

AAP

World.title: Reese accepts Brondello's apology over 'protected species' comment
World.content:
Angel Reese has accepted Australian coach Sandy Brondello's apology for an inappropriate comment about the Atlanta Dream star.

The WNBA suspended Brondello for one game after she was overheard calling Reese a "protected species" during the Dream's 111-92 win over Brondello's Toronto Tempo at the weekend.

"First, I appreciate Sandy's apology, but I also appreciate the love and support that I've had for the last 48 hours," Reese said before the Dream played the Chicago Sky on Monday (AEST).

"It has been very overwhelming with a lot of love and also other things. But I am grateful that the league did take action."

Brondello's comment about Reese was picked up by the broadcast after Toronto player Nyara Sabally went down with an injury and was called for a foul following contact with Reese.

Brondello apologised on social media and Reese posted "ARE WE SURPRISED?!" after the game, tagging Brondello's account, followed by a clown face emoji.

The "protected species" phrase is used in Australian sports to express frustration for a lack of calls against a player. However, in the US, the phrase suggests that someone isn't human and could be seen as derogatory toward Black people.

"There is no place for discrimination or hate in this league from anyone — from fans to coaches to players," Reese said.

"I'm just grateful that we are able to move on from the situation and just play winning basketball. The WNBA is supposed to be positive and we are going in a great light right now, so I just want to continue that and move forward."

Tech.title: AliExpress fined almost $630 million over illegal product sales
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

AliExpress has been hit with a €550 million (about $629 million) fine for violating Europe’s Digital Services Act (DSA) rules by failing to prevent illegal, unsafe, or counterfeit products from being sold on the e-commerce platform. The European Commission ruled that AliExpress didn’t take effective measures to reduce the dissemination of illegal products, noting the company “allocated insufficient staff” to verify products, and failed to remove unsafe toys and dangerous cosmetics for “multiple weeks” after they were detected.

“The spread of counterfeit clothing, unsafe toys, dangerous cosmetics and other illegal and harmful products is not an unavoidable cost of shopping online — it is a failure by AliExpress to comply with its obligations under the Digital Services Act,” EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen said in the announcement. “Scale is not an excuse; risks must be identified and addressed systematically to ensure consumers can safely shop online.”

This is the highest penalty ever imposed under the bloc’s DSA rulebook, followed by rival Chinese retailer Temu, which was also fined more than $230 million for similar DSA infractions in May. AliExpress now has until October 20th 2026 to remedy the breach, or risk facing additional periodic fines.

Tech.title: China delivers a one-two punch to America’s AI dominance
Tech.content:
is a London-based reporter at The Verge covering all things AI and a Senior Tarbell Fellow. Previously, he wrote about health, science and tech for Forbes.

China’s leading AI companies are ramping up the pressure on Silicon Valley, as Moonshot and Alibaba unveiled models they claim can go toe-to-toe with the best from OpenAI and Anthropic at a fraction of the cost. The rapid-fire releases suggest America’s lead at the AI frontier is increasingly tight, just as the technology is becoming central to national security, economic power, and geopolitical influence.

The opening salvo came from Beijing-based Moonshot AI, one of China’s leading AI model developers, which unveiled Kimi K3 on Friday. Moonshot claims its own testing ranks it consistently above nearly every US system, trailing only OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol and Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5, though it came out ahead on certain benchmarks.

Over the weekend, Chinese tech behemoth Alibaba followed with a preview of Qwen3.8, a new model it says is “one of the most powerful model[s] available today” and “second only to Fable 5,” Anthropic’s flagship model.

Both companies are emphasizing a key difference from the leading US labs: Rather than locking their most advanced models behind closed doors, they are making them publicly available. While some US companies, most notably Meta, have taken a similar approach, releasing models that developers can freely download, modify, and build upon has become a growing point of differentiation for China’s AI industry.

Moonshot describes Kimi K3 as the world’s largest open-source AI system, with 2.8 trillion parameters. Parameter counts are measures of a model’s complexity during training and offer a rough indication of its scale and performance, though bigger does not always mean better. Alibaba says Qwen3.8 is a 2.4 trillion parameter model and “continuously evolving.” Neither OpenAI nor Anthropic disclose exact parameter counts for their leading systems.

It remains difficult to assess how capable either Chinese model is until they are fully released and independently tested. Moonshot says it will release full model weights — the internal numerical learned during an AI model’s training period — a week from now on July 27th. Alibaba says Qwen3.8 is “going open-weight soon.”

Even so, the releases have already sharpened competition between the US and China in what has been repeatedly characterized as the defining technological race of our time. They have shaken up the industry in a way not seen since DeepSeek unveiled a low-cost model last year that rivaled leading US systems. The models also raise questions about whether the vast sums of money US companies are pouring into chips, data centers, and model training can secure a durable advantage, particularly if Chinese rivals can approach — or surpass — that frontier with fewer resources.

The prospect of two highly capable Chinese models being released for others to download and adapt also contrasts starkly with the more guarded approach of US labs, whose most advanced systems remain proprietary. That openness emerges even as Washington moves rapidly to restrict global access to the underlying technology. The government has used export controls to restrict China’s access to the most advanced chips, as well as to force Anthropic to pull its most capable system from the market over concerns it could help foreign competitors catch up.

Whether the new Chinese models live up to their creator’s claims remains to be seen. But, like DeepSeek before them, they are likely to sharpen the technological rivalry between the US and China, influence economic and national security policy, and show that America’s lead is far narrower than it once appeared.

Tech.title: This unpronounceable series of glyphs is an incredible side project from Kieran Hebden (aka Four Tet)
Tech.content: is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths. Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed. Just why? ʅ͡͡͡͡͡͡͡͡͡͡͡(̸̢̛̼̞̭͋ͅ)̸͚̰͛̔̾̀̿͒͂:̴͓̞̑̌̂̆̊͋̀:̸͎̟̯̂̓̌ ҉ ͡ ͞ ͞ ͞ ҉● ࿀ ● ࿀ ● ҉⃝ ⃝͢ ͞ ͘ ͞⃝̕ ͢ ̛ ⃝ ̸ ̡ ͢⃝̧ ͡ ͡ ̀ ̧ ̢⃝͜ ҉ ͞ ͞ ⃝͞ ͞ ͡⃝ ⃝҉҈҉҈҉҈҉҈҉҈҉ :̶̢͙͙͕̠̩͆(̷̮͍͚̫͚͂̍)̵̳̗̊( ̟̞̝̜̙̘̗̖҉̵̴̨̧̢̡̼̻̺̹̳̲̱̰̯̮̭̬̫̪̩̦̥ What am I supposed to do with this? It’s un-Googleable. Unpronounceable. It doesn’t even render the same way on various platforms. It looks one way on YouTube Music. Another on Apple Music. And yet another on Bandcamp. Even the artist name ⣎⡇ꉺლ༽இ•̛)ྀ◞ ༎ຶ ༽ৣৢ؞ৢ؞ؖ ꉺლ is an unpronounceable series of glyphs that would make Prince shake his head. So, from here on out, I’m just going to refer to ⣎⡇ꉺლ༽இ•̛)ྀ◞ ༎ຶ ༽ৣৢ؞ৢ؞ؖ ꉺლ by his more well-known alias, Four Tet, and the album as Wingdings. My apologies to Kieran Hebden for disregarding his intent, but I’ve got readers to consider. Also, shoutout to subscriber morgannels for bringing this one to my attention in last week’s what are you listening to thread. ʅ͡͡͡͡͡͡͡͡͡͡͡(̸̢̛̼̞̭͋ͅ)̸͚̰͛̔̾̀̿͒͂:̴͓̞̑̌̂̆̊͋̀:̸͎̟̯̂̓̌ ҉ ͡ ͞ ͞ ͞ ҉● ࿀ ● ࿀ ● ҉⃝ ⃝͢ ͞ ͘ ͞⃝̕ ͢ ̛ ⃝ ̸ ̡ ͢⃝̧ ͡ ͡ ̀ ̧ ̢⃝͜ ҉ ͞ ͞ ⃝͞ ͞ ͡⃝ ⃝҉҈҉҈҉҈҉҈҉҈҉ :̶̢͙͙͕̠̩͆(̷̮͍͚̫͚͂̍)̵̳̗̊( ̟̞̝̜̙̘̗̖҉̵̴̨̧̢̡̼̻̺̹̳̲̱̰̯̮̭̬̫̪̩̦̥ by ⣎⡇ꉺლ༽இ•̛)ྀ◞ ༎ຶ ༽ৣৢ؞ৢ؞ؖ ꉺლ For years, Hebden has kept this alias somewhat of a secret. But now that this collection of wingdings has racked up millions of listens on services like Spotify, it’s get a more formal release with Wingdings. Some of the tracks here have been released previously, including track five, which Fred Again dropped during his incredible Boiler Room set as “Feelings,” under one of Hebden’s other aliases, KH. Wingdings leans heavily toward Four Tet’s dancier outputs. And, despite what the project’s origins as some sort of secret b-side dumping ground might lead you to believe, these are not throwaways. They’re undeniable, infectious, and highly polished. Four Tet’s sense for sound design shines from crushed 8-bit drums to the hypnotic handpan grooves and sharp synth melodies. While the songs are definitely groovy and danceable, they’re not high-octane rave-ups, for the most part. Instead, tracks like number seven build to a more ecstatic and spiritual climax as layers pile up and textures demand you turn your eyes toward the sky. Not unlike last week’s recommendation, Shall We Go On Sinning So That Grace May Increase?, Wingdings is a celebration. No, I might not drop the triphop-esque track one at the club, but it’s perfect for finding your groove while trying to write, or cleaning, or any other activity where you want good vibes and grooves. Track two would feel more at home on a dance floor with its deep four-on-the-floor thump and plucked arpeggios that seem to be constantly climbing off into infinity as house hi-hats tick along. Track three blends metallic gamelan-inspired melodies and ultradeep EDM wubs, while track eight is beautiful comedown ambiance. Four Tet’s Wingdings is available on Bandcamp and most major streaming services, including Apple Music, Spotify, Deezer, and Qobuz.

Tech.title: Kodak EC35 is a dirt-cheap point-and-shoot film camera

is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Following the success of its $99 Kodak-branded Snapic A1, Reto Project is releasing the Kodak EC35, an even more affordable 35mm film camera for just $34.99. The EC35 certainly isn’t fancy. Its 25mm acrylic lens with a fixed f/10 aperture and 1/100 shutter speed basically put it on par with a drugstore disposable. The fact that it has a manual wind and rewind only emphasizes that. And you can really lean into that disposable aesthetic thanks to its built-in automatic flash.

Unlike the A1, there’s no double exposure feature here or zone focusing. The EC35 is designed to require almost no thought to use. Its one special feature is the sliding lens cover, reminiscent of the Olympus Stylus / Mju lineup. It also comes in a bunch of fun colors, including butter yellow, lavender, powder blue, blush pink, and avocado green. The lens covers are a slightly darker shade than the rest of the camera body, giving them some nice subtle contrast. Even the midnight black and vanilla white feature different colored accents, making them slightly more stylish than a disposable camera.

Tech.title: I hate that I don’t hate this song made with Suno
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

I would never go so far as to say there’s no place for AI in music (I’m a fan of Holly Herndon, after all). But I generally find music made with generative AI to be offensively boring, especially the outputs of Suno. So I’m having a bit of a tough time processing the fact that I actually quite enjoy 1010Benja’s “Semiramis’ Dream.”

Benja has been unapologetic about his use of generative AI on his latest EP, Time Has Nothing To Do With What You Choose… The other three tracks can’t quite hold a candle to what you find on 2024’s Ten Total. But the opener “Semiramis’ Dream” is infectious. It explodes out of the speakers with a jungle beat and Benja’s incredible, obviously human voice front and center.

You’d be forgiven for not immediately realizing that the song is the product of Suno. It lacks many of the dead giveaways. Even the most obviously AI part of the song — the choir of backup vocalists — is easily camouflaged amidst the hyperpop-influenced rapid-fire chops. Heavily processed and artificial-sounding vocals are a staple of many modern pop genres and, by leaning into that uncanniness, Benja is able to mask their origins.

But Benja isn’t hiding. He told Hearing Things in an interview:

My friend Patrick Holder did the beat. I recorded the vocals. Then we fed Suno the elements, settled on something, brought it out, edited it on Ableton, and then put it back into Suno. So when you look in Deezer, it marks the song as AI-generated. We’re not hiding it. We don’t feel any shame about it.

Benja’s process certainly separates it from the rest of the Suno slop out there. He wrote the lyrics, sang the vocals, and worked with collaborators to perform the music. Then fed that into Suno, took what the AI spit out, brought it into Abelton, edited it, added more layers, fed that back into Suno… rinse repeat ad naseum. Benja estimates he did this a few hundred times for “Semiramis’ Dream.”

While Benja professes to be agnostic about the tools he uses, he is under no illusion that using generative AI doesn’t come with ethical baggage. He acknowledges the damage it’s doing to the planet, but somewhat nihilistically says we can’t stop greedy corporations or put the AI genie back in the bottle: “The good guy doesn’t win this one,” he says.

The only reason I’m using gen at all is because my visions are currently far beyond my means. People have been asking me, “Did you use gen AI for this EP?” I’m like, [sarcastically] “No, I hired a professional children’s choir.” What are we talking about? I haven’t paid rent last month, and I won’t pay rent this month. I don’t know where the fuck I’m gonna be.

It’s hard not to empathize with Benja. Despite seeming to be on the verge of a breakout and earning a coveted Best New Music from Pitchfork for Ten Total, he’s a struggling artist who has endured periods of homelessness.

Still, it’s also worth acknowledging that there is little on “Semiramis’s Dream” sonically that he couldn’t have achieved without AI. Sure, he couldn’t hire a children’s choir, but it’s not like the AI one found throughout the Time Has Nothing To Do With What You Choose… is particularly convincing. A similar effect could be accomplished with some layered performances and smart vocal processing.

1010Benja hasn’t converted me — I still remain deeply skeptical of AI art. But he has proven that, in the right hands, Suno doesn’t have to be a slop engine.

Tech.title: The FBI reportedly won’t investigate ICE anymore
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

According to the The New York Times, federal agents have been told that the FBI will no longer be investigating confrontations involving ICE agents. The DHS and DOJ denied the change in policy to The Times.

The reported change in guidance follows renewed scrutiny of violence by ICE agents who have killed two people in the last two weeks. The shootings in Maine and Texas were just the latest civilian deaths at the hands of ICE agents, who have attempted to intimidate witnesses following its recent spate of high-profile killings.

The new guidance would end FBI investigations of assaults against DHS agents. The government has aggressively pursued cases against protesters and others who have had even fleeting and unintentional physical contact with agents. But those felony assault cases routinely fall apart, with nearly half of them ending with an acquittal, the charges being thrown out, or withdrawn, according to a Times analysis.

While the FBI investigations are ostensibly to help the government make a case against protesters and others, they often provide evidence against the officers that could be used in future trials against them.

According to The Times:

Under the change, responsibility for investigating cases involving federal immigration officers would likely fall to Homeland Security Investigations, an arm of ICE, effectively leaving the agency to investigate itself…Homeland Security Investigations does not have jurisdiction to investigate civil rights violations, so putting the change into practice would make it far less likely that shootings of unarmed people by ICE agents would be investigated to determine if the agents broke federal law.

Tech.title: Orchid is a delightfully retro and approachable hipster synth
Tech.content:
In 2017, I bought an old Magnus chord organ off Craigslist for $10. It’s one of my favorite music gear purchases. Electric chord organs let you play full chords with just a press of a button, making them perfect for aspiring singer-songwriters or fooling around at home. But chord organs largely fell out of favor in the ’80s, as digital keyboards like those from Casio grew in popularity.

The Telepathic Instruments Orchid attempts to recapture some of that simple parlor instrument magic. Just like those vintage electric chord organs, the Orchid allows you to play rich chord progressions without having to master a ton of theory or complex fingering. It’s not an instrument that demands mastery. It’s a way for songwriters to sketch out ideas with minimal fuss, and it expands on the chord organ heritage with distinctly modern twists.

The Orchid was designed in collaboration with Kevin Parker of Tame Impala. Aesthetically, it harkens back to ’60s brown-and-tan organs by the likes of Magnus and Bontempi. The speaker grill even resembles the fan vents on those classic instruments. It’s definitely a spiritual successor, just, you know, a lot more expensive at $649.

But where a Magnus organ is limited in how many one-button chords it can play by the number of physical reeds it can hold, the Orchid is all digital and can theoretically play any chord, in any voicing, from any scale. It also means that the Orchid can sound like more than just the beautiful droney cousin of an accordion.

Photo: Terrence O’Brien / The Verge

For a songwriter, this means you can focus on your lyrics and vocal melody. If, like me, you struggle to sing and play an instrument at the same time, this can take a huge mental load off. The variety of sounds also means that not everything needs to sound like a funeral dirge or a sea shanty, which isn’t necessarily the case with an old-school chord organ.

If you have even a passing knowledge of music theory (and it would be generous to call mine even passing), you should have little trouble with Orchid. There’s a one-octave keyboard and a handful of buttons to the left of it that correspond to different chord types, i.e., major, minor, diminished, major 7th, and so on. Press C and major, and you get a C major. Press F# and 9, and you get an F#9. Simple.





The Orchid’s E-Piano sound playing chord stabs over a drum beat.(opens a new window) The Orchid’s E-Piano sound playing chord stabs over a drum beat.

The Orchid can really hold your hand if you want it to (and I usually do). You can lock the Orchid to a particular key, so that it will only play chords in the key of E minor or Bb major. That means almost anything you play will at least sound decent and in tune. If your understanding of chord theory is limited, this can really expand your sonic palette with minimal frustration. I often found myself using the chord engine to find a progression I liked as the backbone of a track I could build on top of when jamming in my studio.

But the Orchid can do more than just blast out chords in a single block. It has strum, harp, and arpeggiator modes, plus 13 different preprogrammed patterns. My favorite performance mode (as they’re called) is “slop,” which introduces tiny random timing imperfections that approximate a human actually playing the chord, rather than a machine. The more you turn it up, the more unevenly the notes are struck.





The Orchid’s drum machine and a simple synth pad make a gorgeous combo.(opens a new window) The Orchid’s drum machine and a simple synth pad make a gorgeous combo.

Vintage chord organs have a uniquely droney sound, not unlike a particularly buzzy accordion, that, even 40 years later, was still inspiring artists like El-P. But the Orchid can produce a much broader palette of sounds.

There are three simple synth engines under the hood: one is a virtual analog (VA) synth, another an FM synth for ’80s-style e-pianos and bells, and lastly, a reed piano, perfect for getting those Wurlitzer sounds, but it can also give you more gentle Rhodes electric piano tones as well. I often found myself firing up distorted and heavily reverbed pads on the VA engine and using the Orchid almost like a fidget toy, noodling on simple chord progressions when I needed to focus. You can always connect Orchid to a computer or another synth and use it as a MIDI controller if you want access to its one-key chords but a broader palette of sounds.

Photo: Terrence O’Brien / The Verge

There are 70 presets (excluding bass patches, which we’ll get to in a minute) built into the Orchid, and they cover most of your bases. It’s a good thing, too, since there are very few ways to tweak the sounds directly on Orchid. You can change the filter cutoff or tweak the intensity of effects like reverb or phaser, but that’s basically it. Instead, if you want to design your own patches, you’ll need to spend $99 for the Pistil virtual synth ($50 bundled with the Orchid), which can send custom sounds to Orchid. I’ve found Pistil to be a bit buggy, and the UI often freezes after transferring patches.

Orchid also has a dedicated bass section, separate from the main synth, that you can turn on and off. There are only 12 sounds, but they cover most essentials, from low electric piano octaves to Moog-style synth bass, tuned 808s, and aggressive EDM drones. They can be layered with the main keys to add subtle depth to a chord progression or be played solo.





The Orchid handling both synth arp and bass duties simultaneously. (opens a new window) The Orchid handling both synth arp and bass duties simultaneously.

The accompaniment options are where Orchid can become a bit more complicated than just a simple chord machine. If you don’t lock it to a specific key, and you set the bass to only play along with chords, then you can have the low-end thump locked to your chord progression, and still add melodic flourishes on top without the bass when you’re not pressing any of the chord buttons. Though because of how Orchid handles polyphony — you can’t play multiple keys at once — this can be more frustrating than useful, depending on the patch. If a patch has a long decay time, for instance, chords will cut off abruptly if you try to play a solo note. You’re better off using the built-in audio looper, which lets you record chord progressions, basslines, and melodies separately, for a bit more flexibility.

I am head over heels for the built-in drum machine. It’s extremely limited. You can’t program a custom beat, you can’t tweak the sounds. Yet I think it’s basically perfect, even if it would be nice to have the option for user-uploaded beats from within Pistil. It’s again inspired by vintage gear from the ’70s, namely rhythm machines like the Korg Mini Pops that played preprogrammed beats to accompany home organs. The lo-fi, almost twee sound of these machines is among my favorites in the world of drum machines.





Playing drums, bass, and synth all at the same time on the Orchid. (opens a new window) Playing drums, bass, and synth all at the same time on the Orchid.

The Orchid is fun, sounds good, and is simple to use. But it’s also quite limited. You can’t design your own sounds without paying extra for the Pistil software. The keyboard is small, and you can’t actually play chords on it: You can only play one key at a time, and all the chord voicings come from the chord buttons on the left. That means that if you do know how to play a Dm13 on the piano, for example, you can’t do it on the Orchid’s keyboard. This is a bit of an annoyance, and one of the key differences between it and a vintage chord organ. It varies from model to model, but my personal Magnus organ only has dedicated buttons for Bb, F, C, A, D, and G major chords. Of course, I can always play any chord I want using the Magnus’ regular two-octave keyboard.

Photo: Terrence O’Brien / The Verge

There are far more capable synths in the $649 price range. But the Orchid isn’t trying to compete with the Korg Minilogue or the Arturia MiniFreak. If you want to tinker and design your own synth patches from scratch, spend your money elsewhere. The Orchid isn’t for tinkering. It’s more of a songwriting tool than a synth. If you’re a singer / songwriter looking to escape the cliché of acoustic guitars or upright pianos, the Orchid offers an approachable, if pricey, electronic option.

Tech.title: Hugging Face confirms breach affected internal datasets and credentials, urges users to take action
Tech.content:
Hugging Face, a platform that hosts AI models and datasets, said its internal datasets and service credentials were compromised in a hack last week. The company disclosed the breach on Friday, but said it was still investigating whether any customer or partner data was stolen during the incident.

In a blog post, the company said a dataset uploaded to its platform abused a security vulnerability to run malicious code on its servers, allowing the attackers to escalate their permissions and gain broader access to Hugging Face’s internal systems.

The company said it has revoked and rotated the stolen credentials that were accessed. It urged users to do the same with any keys stored on the platform, and review any suspicious activity on their accounts.

Hugging Face said it has fixed the vulnerability that was abused during the cyberattack. While it’s common for hackers to try to break into a company’s network using stolen employee credentials, keys, or a weak point in their security perimeter, this incident underscores the challenges that companies like Hugging Face face when hackers try to abuse platforms and tools to access and steal sensitive data from within.

Hugging Face blamed the breach on an external AI agent, which executed “many thousands of individual actions across a swarm of short-lived sandboxes, with self-migrating command-and-control staged on public services.”

The company did not immediately provide evidence for this claim when asked by TechCrunch.

Hugging Face said its own anomaly detection spotted the attack, and used an AI model to analyze server logs that kept record of the cyberattack.

The company said it initially used a frontier AI model from a commercial provider, though it didn’t name a company, but found that the analysis effort was blocked by the provider’s guardrails. Instead, the company used its own local large language model, which it said provided the added benefit of not having to upload sensitive attack logs to an AI company’s servers.

Security researchers have previously complained that some frontier models, like Anthropic’s Mythos and Fable, are heavily constrained, and prevent defenders from inquiring about almost anything relating to cybersecurity, including for defense and investigations.

Frontier AI model makers, including Anthropic, have butted heads with the Trump administration over fears and concerns about the ability to use these models for offensive cyberattacks. Anthropic was even forced to withdraw Fable from public use after the U.S. government enforced export controls on the model.

Hugging Face said it has reported the incident to law enforcement and roped in cybersecurity forensic specialists to investigate the breach and review its security.

It’s not clear if Hugging Face had performed a security audit of its systems before it launched. A Hugging Face spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment on Monday.

Tech.title: StrictlyVC returns to New York City September 10 to celebrate a huge year for the city’s startup community
Tech.content:
For the first time since 2024, StrictlyVC is coming back to New York City — and we’re bringing the kind of access you’d expect from an under-wraps event to the whole startup, VC, and dealmaking community.

For years, StrictlyVC has run a series of some of the most interesting nights that a VC, founder, or dealmaker can spend, built around candid conversation you can’t get anywhere else.

Our newly announced NYC event takes place September 10 at Ideal Glass Studios in the West Village, with general admission tickets open now at $180. You can register here.

Why NYC, why now

That’s up from $1.06 billion in H1 2025, with average seed rounds climbing from $5.4 million to $6.64 million.
